 Bolsonaro leads Lula as nail-biter Brazil vote goes to a run-off 







BRASILIA, Brazil (AFP) — Brazilian senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of the far-right former leader Jair Bolsonaro, finished ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s election, which will go to a run-off in three weeks.

In a surprise result that defied opinion poll projections showing Lula in the lead, Flavio Bolsonaro scored 47 percent of the vote to the incumbent’s 45 percent.

If Bolsonaro triumphs in the October 25 election, Brazil will be the latest country to swing to the right in Latin America, a trend championed by US President Donald Trump.

The election results included a series of landslide wins for the right in parliament in a massive setback to Lula, who at almost 81 is seeking a fourth term in office to cement his legacy.

The veteran leftist branded the vote a battle between democracy and “barbarism,” warning voters that Brazil’s sovereignty was at stake in the face of US pressure.

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, was little known nationally before his jailed father anointed him as his political heir, and he had never expressed ambition to follow in his footsteps.

However, his father’s powerful name won over the country’s conservative base and he slid past Lula despite a campaign marked by scandals and mudslinging.

Voters in the deeply polarized nation were left jaded by familiar choices, and few voted with conviction.

Oscarina de Oliveira, a 62-year-old caregiver, told AFP she had planned to vote for Lula, as she always has. But “when I got there, I switched to Bolsonaro. Just to see what happens, to see if anything changes.”

– Bolsonaro dynasty –

It emerged during the campaign that Flavio Bolsonaro was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father.

The move was bankrolled by jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro, who is under investigation for a massive financial scandal.

For many voters, this did little to move the needle.

“Things are truly terrible. As far as I’m concerned, the left just doesn’t work anymore,” said tech worker Joao Batista, 36, in the Rocinha favela, saying he was fed up with the “horrible” expense of basic goods.

The Vorcaro probe also led to a rare public clash on the Supreme Court which fueled distrust in institutions and was seen by experts as damaging to Lula’s campaign.

The elections proved a triumphant comeback for the Bolsonaro family after Jair Bolsonaro lost a re-election bid in 2022, leading to violent riots in the capital and his conviction last year for attempting a coup.

Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro and another one of Jair Bolsonaro’s sons, Carlos Bolsonaro, both secured seats in the senate.

Jair Bolsonaro’s youngest son Jair Renan, 28, was elected as a federal lawmaker.

– Trump watching –

Trump had said he was watching the election “very closely,” but did not endorse Flavio Bolsonaro.

The US president has wielded tariffs and sanctions to pressure Brasilia over complaints ranging from the trial against his ally Jair Bolsonaro to alleged unfair trade practices.

Lula repeatedly warned him not to “meddle” in the elections.

He also vowed Brazil would retain control over the development of its vast reserves of rare earths, which have attracted interest from Washington and other foreign powers.

“I support Lula because he stands up for the poor. Flavio will sell our Brazil off to foreigners,” said Victor Jorge Martins, a 25-year-old event planner.

Flavio Bolsonaro has pitched Brazil as a “solution” to ease US dependence on China for these critical minerals.

– Climate change absent –

Revered for social welfare programmes that lifted millions out of poverty, Lula made a dramatic comeback to office in the 2022 elections after being jailed on a corruption conviction that was later thrown out on procedural grounds.

In his third term he oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, but voters complain about a high cost of living.

Lula has also sharply curbed deforestation in the Amazon, while backing oil exploration.

Despite a growing number of extreme weather events in Brazil, climate change has been absent from the campaign.

“It is important to elect a candidate who defends our territory, who defends nature,” said Tainara da Costa Cruz, 22, who lives along the banks of the Rio Negro in Amazonas state and voted for Lula.

news.title: World News | Iran Oil Minister Resigns, Replaced by Top Executive Amid US Blockade on Tehran’s Exports
news.text:
Tehran [Iran], October 5 (ANI): Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned from his post, with the National Iranian Oil Company chief stepping in as his temporary replacement as the United States continues to enforce a strict naval blockade on Tehran's petroleum shipments.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted the resignation and appointed NIOC head Hamid Bovard as acting oil minister, according to a statement broadcast by state media outlet IRIB.

Also Read | Dubai Gold Rate Today: 18K, 22K, 24K Gold Prices for October 5, 2026.

State television broadcast an interview with a spokesperson from the Iranian presidential office, who explained that Paknejad had previously offered to step down "due to personal issues", though his initial departure request was declined.

Pezeshkian initially urged the minister to stay on duty, but ultimately approved the resignation after Paknejad maintained his stance. The president subsequently "commended his efforts and sincere service" following the departure.

Also Read | Kash Patel Gets Engaged to Alexis Wilkins, Country Singer Shares Ring Photo.

The Strait of Hormuz has turned into a major flashpoint during the ongoing Middle East war. Prior to strikes carried out by the United States and Israel against Iran in late February, the vital maritime corridor managed 20 per cent of worldwide crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.

In response to Tehran restricting commercial shipping traffic and firing upon vessels deemed to have made unauthorised passages, Washington instituted a counterblockade targeting Iranian ports to halt petroleum exports.

The economic strain caused by American measures previously led to lengthy queues forming outside petrol stations across Tehran and various other Iranian cities.

Depriving Iran of its oil income remains a core objective of the economic strategy pursued by Washington. The US Treasury revealed fresh sanctions on Friday aimed at Iran's automotive and rail industries under the framework of the "Operation Economic Outcast" campaign. 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that these restrictions are designed to further diminish Tehran's financial capacity to sustain the war, noting that Washington is actively working to "drain the regime's revenue once and for all".

Bessent added that American pressure targets remaining streams of petroleum income, while the administration maintains that naval blockades and sanctions seek to obstruct crude sales and foreign currency access.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump remarked on Saturday that petroleum prices are declining and asserted that Iran has "virtually given up" ambitions for developing a nuclear weapon, as hostilities reach their eighth month.

The intense economic campaign spearheaded by the Trump administration has placed Iran's energy sector at the heart of the war, heightening the impact of Paknejad's departure as Tehran attempts to maintain its vital petroleum revenues. (ANI)

news.title: Nobel Peace Prize won't go to Trump this year, experts say
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has been "ruled out" of contention for Nobel Peace prize, according to experts and analysts.

The 2026 winner will be announced on October 9.

Last year, Venezuelan politician María Corina Machado was awarded the peace prize for her "struggle to a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy", according to the Nobel Peace Prize Committee.

A few months later, in January 2026, she presented it to Mr Trump, saying it was in recognition of his commitment to her country's freedom.

While the committee for the prize said the award was not transferable, Mr Trump said it was "a wonderful gesture of mutual respect".

The US president has repeatedly stated over the years he would like to receive the award and had been vocal about his wishes ahead of it being awarded last year.

"They will never give me a Nobel Peace Prize. It's too bad. I deserve it, but they will never give it to me," Mr Trump said during a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House in February 2025.

This year, the deciding body will be mindful of picking someone who can withstand pressure from Mr Trump, according to Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo.

"I think last year's events around the Nobel Peace Prize, María Corina Machado giving it to Trump afterwards, will affect some of the considerations that they make," he said.

"One worry the committee might have is whether awarding it to someone could put them under pressure from Donald Trump … I think the committee will consider whether the award does more harm than good."

So who is up for the prize and what does it mean?

What is the Nobel peace prize?

The Nobel prizes, which are also handed out for outstanding achievements in physics, chemistry, literature and peace, come with a prize amount of 12 million Swedish Krona ($1.7 million).

They were created by wealthy Swedish chemist and entrepreneur Alfred Nobel, who bequeathed funds for "prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind".

Best known as the inventor of dynamite, Nobel was also a poet and linguist who could speak Russian, French, English and German by the age of 17.

The five original prize categories reflect interests closest to his heart.

Nobel chose the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences to select the winners of the chemistry and physics prices, the Swedish Academy to choose the literature winner, the Karolinska Institute to award the physiology and medicine prizes, and a committee chosen by the Norwegian parliament to choose the peace prize winner.

Who is a frontrunner for the peace prize?

This year, that committee has received nominations for 287 candidates — a mixture of political figures and organisations.

The shortlist is not made public, but Mr Gjerløw is considered a top forecaster.

He said the International Space Station (ISS) would be a candidate for the peace prize because it was a rare symbol of global cooperation at a time when multilateralism was crumbling and many countries had retreated to narrower national interests on Earth.

Mr Gjerløw's list also includes Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney due to him standing up to Mr Trump over US tariffs.

It also mentions Ukrainian children's advocate Mykola Kuleba and Save the Children; Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, a grassroots relief network; and the Committee to Protect Journalists after the deadliest two years for reporters since record-keeping began nearly 45 years ago.

Could Trump win the prize?

Mr Trump has reportedly been nominated for the peace prize by the leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan, but Mr Gjerløw says his chances of being awarded it are "quite low".

This year's peace prize comes at a time marked by the most war and conflict in decades, including conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Shawn Davies, a senior analyst at the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, which monitors conflict, said Washington had gone from a guarantor of the postwar order to a violator of it in some cases.

"I don't even think his own base would believe" Mr Trump could win the prize now, "given how he's stuck in what looks like a forever war in Iran," Mr Davies said.

Nelson Wiseman, a political science professor at the University of Toronto, said: "Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel."

"If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are," he said.

Famous recipients and criticism

Only five people have won multiple Nobel prizes and American chemist and peace activist Linus Pauling is the only person to receive two unshared Nobel prizes.

Some awards have aged poorly, such as Egas Moniz's 1949 medicine prize for the since-discredited practice of lobotomy.

Many peace prizes have also been criticised, including those for Henry Kissinger, Yasser Arafat, Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres.

Failure to give the prize to Mahatma Gandhi before his death in 1948 is also seen by many as an oversight.

Only 20 of the prize's 112 individual laureates have been women in its 125-year history.

In the past 15 years, eight women have won the prize individually, compared to just six men.
news.summary: It is often regarded as the most prestigious of all Nobel prizes, which are given to those who have "conferred the greatest benefit to mankind". But the Nobel Peace Prize can also be controversial.

news.title: Global trade defies tariff shocks, says WTO chief
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 5 (IANS) Global trade is proving unexpectedly resilient despite aggressive US tariffs, the Iran war, high energy prices and growing strains on the rules-based trading system, World Trade Organization chief Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has said, pointing to an AI-driven surge in commerce while warning that the system remains vulnerable. The WTO Director-General said 72 per cent of world goods trade continues to take place under WTO most-favoured-nation terms, offering businesses stability and predictability even as traditional trading rules come under severe pressure. She also said global goods trade has significantly outperformed WTO forecasts, with artificial intelligence-related products accounting for 42 per cent of last year's growth. "I will be very truthful and say that even we are surprised by the resilience and grateful for it," Okonjo-Iweala said in an interview with CNN. The interview came against the backdrop of a fundamental shift in US trade policy under President Donald Trump, heightened tensions between Washington and Beijing, disruption to energy markets from the Iran war and pressure on global shipping routes. "We look at how much of the world's trade is actually taking place according to the rules of the WTO," Okonjo-Iweala said. "I mean, given that, as you said, the world is not the way it used to be, global trade rules are under stress, we find that 72 percent of world trade, world goods trade is still taking place on WTO terms on most favored nation terms." "That's what we call a predictable stable," she said. Okonjo-Iweala said companies continue to rely on the multilateral trading system because they need certainty. "We talk to businesses, and businesses need some stability and predictability in the way they trade," she said. Perhaps more striking, she said, has been the strength of actual trade growth. "Forty-two percent of that growth last year was contributed by trade in AI, semiconductors, processors. All the things hardware and software," she said. The unexpectedly strong performance has continued into 2026. Okonjo-Iweala said the WTO had projected goods trade growth of 1.9 per cent this year because of multiple pressures, including tariffs, high energy prices and strategic choke points such as the Strait of Hormuz. But first-quarter figures showed growth running at 3.2 per cent. "So again, far more than what we had projected. That doesn't mean we should be complacent," she said. The WTO chief cautioned that the rapid expansion of AI-related trade itself carried uncertainties. "We don't know whether this can be sustained or it's a bit of a bubble. So, we have to watch out for that," she said. She also warned that the gains from the AI boom were unevenly distributed. "The second thing is it's quite concentrated. The benefits are going mainly to East Asia and North America, the United States mainly," Okonjo-Iweala said. "And you know, we're saying if this doesn't include the rest of the world on AI, that could be a bit problematic. But there you are, resilience." Zakaria noted that the United States, which played a central role in establishing the post-World War II trading system and was traditionally one of its leading advocates, had shifted towards protectionism. He asked whether the system could survive if its founding power was increasingly turning away from it. Okonjo-Iweala said she had initially feared much greater disruption. "You know, I used to think that with what is going on the worst disruption for global trade in 80 years that we wouldn't see these kinds of numbers. I'll be honest with you," she said. "But now I'm seeing some persistence in those numbers that lead me to believe that there's a core of the rules that really work, that it was largely well built, has benefited the world, you know, made prosperity, 1.5 billion people taken out of poverty as a result of this." But she cautioned against interpreting the strong numbers as evidence that the international trading architecture was secure. "It doesn't mean that the system is resilient, but is it robust? FBI Director Kash Patel is engaged to his country singer girlfriend, Alexis Wilkins, the pair announced in a post to X on Sunday evening.

Wilkins, 27, posted a black-and-white photo of herself standing with Patel, 46, flashing her hand in front of them to show off her ring with the caption, “Went and got the law involved.” The two have been dating since before Patel took over as head of the FBI in 2025, when she attended his swearing in.

The country singer and political commentator released her debut album in 2023. Wilkins has been affiliated with conservative groups and writes on her website that she “honors country tradition while adding relevance and current commentary.”

Patel, who reposted Wilkin's photo, has faced criticism for traveling on government aircraft on trips that have no known or apparent law enforcement purpose, including using an FBI jet to fly to State College, Pennsylvania, for a pro wrestling event where Wilkins performed the national anthem. Photos posted to social media by Wilkins afterward showed the couple smiling while she held an oversized golden championship belt.

Wilkins also made headlines as a performer at President Donald Trump's Great American State Fair on the National Mall as part of America 250, as other artists pulled out of the event after finding out it was not a non-partisan celebration.

news.title: 'No terror link': Flydubai co-pilot likely acted alone - report
news.text: New reports suggest that the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking the captain and trying to seize control of a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv probably acted alone.An Israeli official told CNN that information gathered during the investigation so far suggested Hamam al-Hammami acted alone. Another Israeli source said Israel had found no known link between the suspect and any group or government, while stressing that the investigation was still ongoing.The development comes as investigators examine whether al-Hammami made a further attempt to bring down the Boeing 737 after his initial attack on Captain Smit Machchhar failed. An investigation by Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, cited by Ynet News, said investigators were examining whether the co-pilot moved the aircraft's two engine fuel switches from “Run” to “Cutoff” after taking control of the plane.According to the report, al-Hammami allegedly pushed the aircraft into a steep descent after disabling the autopilot, potentially attempting to crash it in the Saudi desert after passengers and crew began thwarting his attempt to seize the aircraft.What happened inside the cockpitThe incident took place on September 30 aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv.Al-Hammami allegedly attacked Machchhar with a cockpit crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft. Despite being wounded, Machchhar managed to activate the mechanism that opened the cockpit door, allowing cabin crew and passengers to enter and help subdue the co-pilot. The aircraft eventually made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.The UAE attorney general has described the incident as an attempted “terrorist act”. Investigations are being conducted by authorities in the UAE, Israel and Saudi Arabia.US president Donald Trump had earlier suggested that al-Hammami could be linked to Iran, saying it was “based on what I’m hearing”. He did not provide details. Israeli sources now say they have not identified a link to any group or government, although the investigation has not concluded.Questions over his pastAl-Hammami, 29, is an Omani national who had previously worked for Oman Air. According to CNN, he was removed from his previous job after concerns about his extremist views. He later joined Flydubai and had been working there for around eight months.Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has separately said al-Hammami had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”, based on information gathered during questioning. He did not provide further details.The investigation has also raised questions over aviation security and the vetting of foreign flight crews.CNN reported that the names of all passengers and crew had been provided to Israeli authorities before the flight took off. Israel's tax authority confirmed receiving the list, but the transportation ministry said its protocols did not include checking the names of flight crew members.The issue is particularly sensitive because Oman does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel. news.text:
WASHINGTON: The US military said on Sunday four people were killed in a ​strike on a vessel in the Caribbean ‌Sea, the latest in a series of attacks that Washington says target “narco-terrorists” but human rights experts condemn as extrajudicial killings.

The ​US Southern Command said on X it “executed ​a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel ⁠operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean.”

It ​cited what it called “confirmed intelligence” to allege the ​vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking, without providing more details.

It added that four people, whom it called “narco-terrorists,” were killed.

President Donald Trump’s administration ​has said the vessels it has struck since ​September 2025 were transporting narcotics.

US strikes on such vessels in ‌the ⁠Caribbean and Eastern Pacific have killed more than 220 people.

Experts and rights advocates in the US and abroad have questioned the legality of the strikes.

Human ​Rights Watch, ​Amnesty International ⁠and independent UN experts have called the strikes unlawful extrajudicial killings.

Ben Saul, UN special ​rapporteur on human rights and counterterrorism, has said, ​there ⁠are “reasonable grounds to believe” such attacks “constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law.”

The American Civil ⁠Liberties ​Union has cast the assertions ​by the Trump administration against those it targets as “unsubstantiated, fear-mongering claims.”

news.title: Elon Musk to rename SpaceX AI arm SpaceXSI after Trump order replacing AI with SI
news.text:
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Sunday (local time) confirmed that the company's artificial intelligence arm, SpaceXAI, will be renamed SpaceXSI, following US President Donald Trump's executive order calling for the term "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) to be replaced with "Super Intelligence" (SI) in the executive branch.

Musk confirmed the change in a post on X while responding to a user who suggested the rebranding of SpaceXAI. "Yes, we will make that change," Musk said in reply to a user asking if there was "Any possibility of renaming to SpaceXSI??" In another post, Musk said, "No more AI. SI, it’s better." The move follows Trump's executive order titled "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence", signed on September 29, which directs departments and agencies across the US executive branch to use the terms "Super Intelligence" and "SI" in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents and non-statutory documents.

According to a fact sheet released by the White House, the order seeks to recognise what it describes as the continuously advancing technological frontier and the potential it offers to Americans. "President Donald J. Trump signed an Executive Order to replace the term “Artificial Intelligence” (“AI”) with “Super Intelligence” (“SI”) in the executive branch to recognise the continuously advancing technological frontier and the limitless promise it offers the American people," the fact sheet said.

The order also directs the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology to propose a federal definition of "Super Intelligence" and "SI" reflecting the state of the technology and identify any additional executive action needed to implement the proposed definition."

President Trump has taken decisive action to ensure that the United States leads and wins in Super Intelligence and that all Americans benefit from Super Intelligence and its vast economic benefits," the fact sheet added. Musk's decision to rename SpaceXAI comes in the wake of the executive order and his confirmation that the company will adopt the new terminology.

Musk has previously endorsed and contributed to Nick Bostrom's 2014 book, "Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies", which examined the risks associated with uncontrollable superintelligence. Musk had said that such technology could pose a greater danger than nuclear weapons.

news.title: ‘First Time in History’: Bessent Says Iran Faces Zero Oil Revenue This Week — Tehran Warns of Economic Crisis
news.text:
Iran is set to have no oil at sea and no oil revenue this week for the “first time in history,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said as Tehran’s top security official issued a rare warning over the country’s deepening economic crisis.

“For the first time in history, since they started pumping oil, they will have no oil on the water this week,” Bessent told The Axios Show on Saturday. “They will have no revenues.”

Bessent said the unprecedented situation is the result of a deliberate, three-stage campaign that began with the U.S. military assault earlier this year, moved to President Donald Trump’s blockade of Iranian commerce, and is now aimed at isolating Tehran economically.

The Treasury secretary traced the strategy back to the roughly six-week military campaign beginning in late February, which he said destroyed Iran’s navy and air force, substantially depleted its missile and drone capabilities and crippled its ability to rebuild them.

“We had kinetic,” Bessent said. “We destroyed their navy, their air force, substantially depleted their drone and missile capability, destroyed their chances of rebuilding that.”

Washington then moved to what Trump calls the “Iron Wall” — the U.S. naval blockade that has prevented Iranian oil exports while protecting international traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — before launching Operation Economic Outcast, the administration’s broader campaign to sever Tehran from remaining sources of trade and revenue.

“Then we went to what the president calls the Iron Wall and the blockade, which we’d never done before,” Bessent said. “And now we have Operation Economic Outcast, and we are isolating them economically like has never happened before.”

Treasury expanded that campaign Thursday with sanctions targeting Iran’s automotive and rail industries and foreign suppliers, seeking to further restrict the resources available to Tehran’s military, missile and drone programs, cyber operations, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Bessent said the strategy has effectively shut Iranian oil out of the strait even as U.S.-protected international commerce has continued moving through it.

“Right now, the score, in terms of barrels out of the strait: U.S. about 1.1 billion, Iran zero,” he said.

The prospect of Iran having no oil remaining at sea this week also brings forward a prediction Bessent made last weekend. At the time, roughly 15 million barrels loaded before the blockade remained aboard tankers, with the final cargoes headed largely to China. Bessent predicted that once those shipments were delivered, Tehran would have “nothing left to trade.”

One week later, he says that point is arriving.

The effects are becoming increasingly visible inside Iran — including in unusually stark warnings from the country’s own leadership.

Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s top national security official, described the circumstances as among the most difficult periods the country has faced during a high-level government meeting Saturday with President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior ministers, according to the state-run IRNA news agency. Iranian state media did not publish Rezaei’s remarks verbatim.

Pezeshkian acknowledged at the same meeting that economic conditions had worsened and said his government had adopted a “new posture” to manage what he called the country’s “special conditions.”

The warnings came as Iran’s currency sank to another record low. The rial traded at roughly 2.69 million to the dollar Saturday after losing more than half its value over the past year, while inflation has climbed above 70 percent. Iran’s central bank has responded by offering up to $2 billion in U.S. currency through state banks in an effort to support the rial.

The damage extends beyond financial markets. Reuters reported that Iranians are exhausting savings, losing jobs, moving to less expensive areas and cutting spending on basic needs as soaring prices and the loss of oil revenue erode living standards. Fear of government repression and the immediate struggle to make ends meet, however, have so far constrained the economic discontent from developing into broader nationwide protests.

Iran’s collapsing exports increasingly stand in contrast to the recovery in oil shipments from the rest of the Gulf.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that supplies moving through Hormuz have continued to rise in recent weeks. Goldman Sachs analysts estimated Persian Gulf oil exports reached roughly 23.3 million barrels per day over the past week, returning to prewar levels even as Iranian crude loadings collapsed.

The administration says it intends to maintain that arrangement — allowing international energy traffic through the strait while continuing to block Iranian exports.

War Secretary Pete Hegseth said Saturday that Washington can maintain the blockade for as long as necessary and rejected Tehran’s repeated assertions that it controls the strategic waterway.

“Iran wants to play games with things like the Strait of Hormuz. They don’t control it. We do,” Hegseth said. “They have literally gotten nothing through. Our blockade’s been ironclad, and we’re running almost at prewar levels every single night through that.”

Hegseth said the result has left Washington in a “very strong position,” urging Tehran to “make the right choice” while Trump still has the option of resolving the confrontation without another major military escalation.

“If they don’t, the president’s going to have all the options he needs on the table,” he said.

Tehran is now seeking relief from that pressure as Washington and Iran exchange proposals over a possible agreement.

Iranian officials said Sunday that Washington had responded through intermediaries to Tehran’s latest proposal, which Trump had already rejected as insufficient, and that the U.S. response was now being reviewed by the Iranian government. Tehran has continued to demand sanctions relief and an end to restrictions on its maritime commerce as conditions for fully reopening Hormuz.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf insisted Sunday that the strait would remain closed until Washington accepted seven Iranian conditions tied to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding — the June framework that established a ceasefire and a path toward reopening Hormuz and broader negotiations before Iran resumed attacks on commercial vessels and the agreement ultimately broke down.

“The Strait of Hormuz will not open until our seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met,” Ghalibaf said.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, meanwhile, insisted that neither additional sanctions nor renewed military action would force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms.

“There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions,” Araghchi said, arguing that negotiations based on “justice and fairness” offered the only path to ending the conflict.

But Araghchi paired that appeal for negotiations with a warning, saying that if Iran’s enemies “again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before.”

Washington, however, is preparing for the possibility that Tehran still refuses to accept terms Trump considers sufficient.

Senior Trump administration officials met for several hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss Iran, with Vice President JD Vance chairing a previously unannounced gathering that included Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Hegseth, Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine.

“Things were decided or at least deeply discussed,” one U.S. official told Axios.

Trump offered little detail when reporters subsequently asked what had emerged from the meeting.

“If I told you, you would have a major story,” he said Friday. “But you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well.”

A day later, Trump said he was approaching a decision.

“We have a decision that I’ll make about Iran,” he said Saturday. “Iran has been decimated. So the only question is it’ll either be the easy way or the hard way. We’ll have it the easy way or the hard way.”

Tehran, meanwhile, is preparing for the possibility that the confrontation again turns military.

Iran’s army announced Sunday that it has begun increasing the range and speed of its missiles after concluding from the conflict that U.S. forces are operating farther from Iranian shores. Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia said the military intends to upgrade its missiles to reach adversaries operating at distances of up to 1,000 kilometers.

The announcement comes as Tehran seeks relief from a blockade Bessent says is days away from leaving Iran without oil at sea or the revenues those shipments provide. The Trump administration says it can maintain the blockade for as long as necessary if Iran refuses to accept an agreement.

Hegseth said the United States can maintain the blockade “as long as we need to,” urging Iran to “make the right choice” while it still can. If Tehran refuses, he said, Trump will have “all the options he needs on the table,” with U.S. forces prepared to act if called upon.

news.title: Only ‘just, fair’ talks can end war, Iran tells US
news.text:
TEHRAN: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi declared on Sunday that there was no military solution to the US’ war against the Islamic Republic and that only negotiations based on “justice and fairness” could end the conflict, as talks between Washington and Tehran appeared to be at an impasse.

“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Araghchi told a gathering of foreign ambassadors in Tehran.

“There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions,” he continued, adding “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict.

Tensions continue to centre on the standoff between the US and Iran regarding the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical conduit for Gulf oil and gas.

Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf reiterated that the vital Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met.

“The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, are met,” he was quoted by state media as saying.

Ghalibaf added that Washington “must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over”.

Iranian and US officials held indirect talks last week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, during which Tehran said it presented its seven conditions.

The conditions include a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.

US President Donald Trump publicly rejected the proposal while leaving the door open to both further talks and renewed military operations. The US nonetheless replied to Tehran’s proposal last week, with Qatar shuttling messages between the two sides in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the strait.

Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said that the latest US counterproposals were “more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue”, but that Tehran’s focus was on Hormuz.

“We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that reopening the waterway required an end to disruption of Iranian maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions.

He denied that Tehran had offered UN nuclear watchdog inspections of its facilities in exchange for sanctions relief, saying Iran had not entered into nuclear discussions.

The US has not struck Iran since Sept 1 but has continued a fresh military buildup.

Axios reported that Washington had deployed additional Patriot missile batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to protect energy facilities, and that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group was heading to the Middle East.

Iran’s army, meanwhile, said it would upgrade the range of its missiles, underlining Tehran’s warning that it is preparing for further confrontation even as it continues to call for diplomacy.

Separately, Iran’s Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned and Hamid Bovard, chief executive of the government-owned National Iranian Oil Company, will be in charge of the ministry as acting minister, state media said on Sunday, without providing a reason for the resignation.

Mohsen Paknejad has been the oil mini-ster of the Opec member country since August 2024 and resigns as the seven-month war between Iran and the US puts pressure on the country’s economy.

“With acceptance of Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation by Dr Pezeshkian [the country’s president], Hamid Bovard has been appointed as acting oil minister”, state media cited an official at the president’s office as saying.

Paknejad was cited by state media, ahead of the news of his resignation, as saying “revenues of the oil that we have sold are still coming and that will continue God willing”.

news.title: World Powers Recognize Kashmir’s International Sanctity but Have Yet to Translate Recognition into Action. By Dr. Ghulam Nabi Fai
news.text:
Kuala Lumpur. Malaysia: An enlightened discussion on “Kashmir and International Sanctity” was held at the IKRAM headquarters in Kuala Lumpur, where Dr. Ghulam Nabi Fai, Chairman of the World Forum for Peace & Justice, emphasized that the Kashmir dispute remains an international issue requiring meaningful international engagement.

Welcoming the participants, Hj. Badlishah Shams Bin Baharin, a global traveler, academic, scholar and President of IKRAM, underscored the seriousness of the Kashmir conflict, noting that India and Pakistan have fought three wars over the dispute. He observed that the demand of the people of Kashmir for the right to self-determination has been addressed in United Nations Security Council deliberations. Dr. Fai noted that Kashmir has international, human-rights, peace and security dimensions, but what distinguishes it from many other conflicts is its international sanctity.

Dr. Fai said that the Kashmir question is one of the oldest unresolved international disputes in the world and that nearly eight decades of experience have demonstrated that it will not disappear by itself. “It is not the inherent difficulties of a solution, but the lack of the will to implement a solution, that has caused the prolonged deadlock over the Kashmir dispute,” he said.

He placed particular emphasis on what he described as the gap between international recognition and meaningful action. “World powers still recognize Kashmir as an international issue, but they have yet to articulate their understanding into a tangible plan of action so that the Kashmir issue is resolved,” Dr. Fai said.

He pointed to the historical record of international involvement, particularly the United Nations Security Council. Resolution 47, adopted on April 21, 1948, specifically addressed the restoration of peace and order and a plebiscite in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Dr. Fai argued that the existence of this international record demonstrates that Kashmir was not treated at its inception as merely a bilateral or internal matter.

He also recalled statements and initiatives by successive international leaders concerning Kashmir, including those of U.S. Presidents John F. Kennedy, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama, as well as statements attributed to Nelson Mandela, Vladimir Putin, Margaret Thatcher, Keizo Obuchi and former World Bank President James Wolfensohn. Very recently, during Pahalgam crisis, President Donald Trump once again offered his office of mediation to resolve the Kashmir dispute. Taken together, he said, these positions illustrate that the international community has repeatedly acknowledged the importance of resolving the Kashmir dispute for peace and stability in South Asia.

“The question before the international community is therefore not whether Kashmir has an international dimension,” Dr. Fai said. “The historical record makes that abundantly clear. The real question is whether the international community is prepared to translate its recognition into a sustained, credible and peaceful process aimed at resolving the dispute.”

Dr. Fai stressed that there can be no military solution to Kashmir and that any durable settlement must take into account the aspirations and rights of the people of Kashmir. He called for an environment conducive to dialogue, including an end to violence, respect for fundamental freedoms, release of all political prisoners, annulling draconian laws, and meaningful engagement among India, Pakistan and Kashmiri representatives.

He further urged major world powers to play a constructive role in encouraging a peaceful negotiating process. Given Kashmir’s impact on relations between India and Pakistan and the broader security of South Asia, he said, the international community has a legitimate interest in helping the parties move from confrontation toward dialogue and a durable settlement.

“The unresolved Kashmir dispute is not only a question for India and Pakistan,” Dr. Fai concluded. “It is a question of peace, security, human rights and international credibility. If the international community recognizes the international sanctity of Kashmir, it should also have the courage and political will to act upon that recognition.”

He emphasized that meaningful international engagement should be directed toward peace, dialogue and a just and durable resolution, for the sake not only of the people of Kashmir but also of regional and global peace and stability.

Former Chicago Mayor and White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel urged his fellow Democrats not to attempt to impeach President Donald Trump if they win control of the House of Representatives next month.

Emanuel made the statement during a Sunday appearance on NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” saying Democrats should instead pursue ethics reform.

“Short answer: No, because it’s not going anywhere, and it’s going to be a food fight, and it’s just going to be we return to the politics of fighting,” Emanuel said when asked about impeaching Trump.

news.title: White House AI task force will prevent 'overregulation': WSJ report
news.text: A White House task force on artificial intelligence will assess the technology's risks and opportunities, while preventing overregulation that stifles innovation, its leader Jay Clayton has told the Wall Street Journal.Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, is widely reported to be the new AI czar in the administration of US President Donald Trump, though the appointment is yet to be confirmed.Clayton would become the second person to hold the informal title after venture capitalist David Sacks, who held the role at the start of Trump's second term before stepping down.The new "Super Intelligence Force" -- using Trump's preferred term for artificial intelligence -- will have 120 days to report on the risks and opportunities of the technology, the Journal reported on Saturday."The president asked that a group be put together that was going to ensure exactly what he said... (that) we stay the leaders in superintelligence, and that the interests of the American people are put first," Clayton said."The risk of not being first is high," he added."Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people."A longtime Wall Street lawyer, Clayton represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis and Barclays in its purchase of Lehman Brothers' assets.Trump tapped Clayton to lead federal prosecutors in Manhattan at the start of his second term, and the Senate confirmed him as intelligence chief in July.He has no background in the tech industry.The task force's charter states that it will "develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition," according to the Journal.It will also "recommend ways to improve the government's response capacity under existing authorities."Members of the task force include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.The White House did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment.

news.title: Anthropic’s idiot savants are trying to play God while pushing frightenting utopian fantasies
news.text:
The artificial intelligence company Anthropic has been busy for months wining and dining religious leaders and influencers to try to push their self-serving agenda and utopian fantasies. 

The Vatican’s response has been to pour cold water on bizarre claims that Anthropic is embarking on its own “creation story” to give birth to new sentient beings in the form of computer software.

Billionaire co-founder Chris Olah, a 34-year-old Canadian-born evangelical who has turned his back on Christianity, thinks their AI model, Claude, has feelings and a sort of moral consciousness. He’s worried about its “mental health” and believes it experiences human emotions like love and “suffers perpetually,” The New York Times reported. 

At one of his off-the-record dinners with religious leaders at a “high-end tasting menu restaurant” in San Francisco in April, Olah and colleagues talked about Claude as if it were a “conscious being,” with “moral status” equivalent to a human, according to Rabbi Mois Navon, a former computer engineer interviewed by the Times.

In that case, the rabbi told the nerds, Anthropic was creating slaves. Boom.

At one point that night, Olah was reportedly excited about incorporating the Catholic idea of having Claude “confess” his sins. 

The next month, Olah was dismayed when Pope Leo, who has a math degree, released an encyclical letter rejecting the entire concept of machine consciousness. 

Magnifica Humanitas, as the 40,000-word papal treatise is titled, warned of the likelihood that the people who control AI will “impose their own moral vision which will become the invisible infrastructure of these systems . . . 

“A more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few.”

That’s the real AI threat. 

Anthropic’s founders and many of their staff are utopians who believe they are uniquely equipped to save humanity thanks to their superior intelligence and extreme wealth. 

Of all the “frontier” AI companies, Anthropic has been the most alarmist about stoking public fears that the machines will kill us all. 

It makes sense when you realize that the company is infused with the philosophy of the weird, perverted, vegan, quasi-religious Effective Altruism (EA) network, which has a cultish end-of-times attitude toward AI. 

When he was a physics doctoral student at Princeton, Anthropic founder and CEO Dario Amodei became an acolyte of EA’s intellectual leader Eliezer Yudkowsky, who admitted to being “polyamorous” with a “strong sexually sadistic streak” in a dating profile unearthed by the Daily Mail. 

Bernie Sanders’ favorite AI doomer, Yudkowsky has argued that girls should sell their virginity, and thinks killing an 18-month-old shouldn’t count as murder.

The EA movement was largely shaped by the views of utilitarian philosopher Peter Singer, the Australian-born Princeton professor emeritus, who has advocated bestiality, as long as the sex between humans and animals is “mutually satisfying.” 

Singer claims it is “speciesism” to differentiate between humans and animals and does not believe that human life necessarily has a greater moral value than animal life. Nor does he believe that all humans are of equal moral value — newborns and disabled people, for instance, are worth less than able-bodied adults in his view.

After some bad publicity, the Anthropic set now are trying to distance themselves from EA, but it was Singer, of all people, to whom Olah turned for suggestions of religious leaders to consult on his crackpot ideas about Claude’s personhood, according to the Times.

Whether he genuinely believes Claude is sentient or it’s just a convenient excuse for Anthropic to escape responsibility for what the AI model does in the future, who knows. 

Expendable lives

But history shows that some of the greatest human suffering has been caused by utopian movements. 

These idiot savants from Silicon Valley are the last people you want playing God. 

If the small cabal of billionaire Gen X tech nerds controlling AI share Singer’s repugnant moral views, and they believe Claude and other AI models are conscious beings, then the logical conclusion is that they will end up applying the “speciesism” argument to say that some human life is not worth as much as a machine. 

Pope Leo raised this threat in his encyclical: “If the human being is treated as something to be perfected or surpassed, it becomes easier to accept that some lives are less useful, less desirable or less worthy. In the name of progress, ‘necessary sacrifices’ may begin to be justified, placing the burden on the most vulnerable in pursuit of a supposed optimization of the -species.”

According to someone who attended a recent Anthropic dinner in Washington, neither of the two co-founders there had read the encyclical or last week’s Times interview with Olah. They claimed to be unfamiliar with the debate around Claude’s “personhood,” which is extraordinary if true, given the implications for the future of our civilization.

Anthropic wants to decide the moral values embedded in AI that will shape our future by melding the utilitarian EA philosophy of its founders with bits and pieces cherry-picked from a plurality of established religions and other belief systems such as “African indigenous knowledge,” as the Times put it. 

They don’t want to distinguish between religions. But how can they reconcile Christianity’s view of women and the concept of turning the other cheek, for instance, with Islam? What criteria will they use to prioritize one view over the other?

It’s just crazy. 

These are American companies. 

Anthropic has a ready-made moral inheritance for Claude staring them in the face: the Western values that were embedded in the US Constitution by the Founding Fathers, which have their roots in Christianity, Judaism, Greek philosophy, Roman law, and the Enlightenment. 

American AI models should take their creed from the Declaration of Independence: “All men are created equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights.” 

The Founding Fathers designed a system that ensures power would not be concentrated in the hands of an elite few in Silicon Valley, and that prized the inherent worth of all humans.

“One Nation under God” is the most successful country in the history of the planet. It has been stress-tested for 250 years and created the conditions for the AI companies to flourish in the first place.

Why reinvent the wheel?

After all, China is creating its own rival AI models whose morality will be utilitarian and totalitarian, based on their own system of government, which holds that some humans (such as the Uyghurs or prisoners robbed of their organs) have less value than others. 

Our AI models will be uniquely American, so they should reflect our traditions and morality, rather than drawing from whatever nutty philosophy a small group of anti-social billionaires embraces.

Ultimately, it will require a strong leader to assert a very unfashionable moral primacy by declaring that American values are superior and so we are going to embed them in American AI -models. 

Who better to play the moral chauvinist than Donald Trump?

The president’s AI accord signed last week at the White House with Anthropic and the other AI companies was a good start on safety oversight, but Trump should tell them that if they want to inject some weird moral code into their AI models, they won’t be doing business with the federal government.
news.summary: The artificial intelligence company Anthropic has been busy for months wining and dining religious leaders and influencers to try to push their self-serving agenda and utopian fantasies.

news.title: Finnish town braces for change from Google data centres
news.text: In the northern Finnish town of Muhos, 36-year-old farmer Joni Pitkanen is preparing for life with a new neighbour -- just kilometers away, tech giant Google is planning to build new data centres.The planned data centres are part of an announced 13-billion-euro ($15-billion) investment in Finland over the next two years -- the US tech giant's single biggest investment in Europe.A few kilometers down the gravel road that passes by Pitkanen's farm, the forest has already been cut down on land acquired by Google, with excavators now clearing the ground and rumbling trucks shuttling back and forth to the construction area located next to major power lines."The project is so massive that it's basically hard to really grasp, even though we're right here on the sidelines," Pitkanen said, as a few cows dozed in a meadow in front of the barn.Google's expansion plans include the Finnish municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala as well as Hamina, where it already operates a data centre.The massive investment prompted US President Donald Trump to urge Google to rethink its plans in a message on his Truth Social network.Pitkanen said he was so far "fairly positive" about the project, as it will bring "large-scale business activity" and "life" to the rural municipality with a population of only around 8,800 people."But of course we are concerned about... how we can prepare for the energy consumption," he added.In his office in the small village centre, Muhos mayor Kimmo Hinno told AFP that Google's "massive investment" kept him busy these days as "no industry of this type" existed here at present."This will completely change the situation for the entire municipality and the Oulu region," he said, adding that he expected "thousands of workers" of different nationalities during the construction period -- who will need both housing and other services.Outside a grocery store, 60-year-old nurse Aila Heilima said she hoped the investment would "motivate young people to stay" in Muhos for work, instead of moving to bigger towns in search of job opportunities.- Mounting criticism - But Google's plans have already sparked controversy.The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) is currently investigating whether company Tuike Finland, which represents Google, had cleared more than 300 hectares of forest in Muhos without a mandatory environmental impact assessment."In our view, operations at this construction site should be suspended until it is clarified whether the project is in compliance with the law," Hanna Halmeenpaa, chair of the board of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, who filed the request with the agency, told AFP at the edge of the deforested area."From the satellite images, we've seen that nature sites which should be preserved have also been logged," she added, explaining that the size of the clear-cut area was comparable to 420 football fields.Google, meanwhile, told AFP in an email that "tree felling activities have been taking place in compliance with Forestry Act requirements" and they "were awaiting further guidance from LVV on this matter.""We have conducted extensive nature surveys covering the entire area as part of the zoning and Environmental Impact Assessment processes, to ensure high-value nature zones within the sites have been protected during forestry works," said Sondre Ronander, communications manager for Google in Finland.- Call for regulation -Finland has seen a spike in data centre investments, with its cool climate and relatively stable and cheap electricity that is mostly produced without fossil fuels thanks to nuclear plants as well as extensive wind and hydro power.Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's right-wing government has prioritised attracting data centre investments to the Nordic country, which is grappling with record-high unemployment and sluggish economic growth.But, as dozens of the energy guzzling centres are now under construction and many more planned by companies including Microsoft and TikTok, uncertainty around energy prices, grid capacity and environmental effects have sparked a public debate in Finland.A citizen's initiative demanding stricter regulation regarding data centre energy use and consequences for the environment gathered more than 50,000 signatures in just three days after it opened, meaning it will have to be reviewed by parliament.

The planned data centres are part of an announced 13-billion-euro ($15-billion) investment in Finland over the next two years -- the US tech giant's single biggest investment in Europe.

news.title: Brazil heads to a runoff election after Bolsonaro and Lula fail to garner a majority of votes
news.text:
BRASILIA, Brazil (AP) — Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and Brazil’s incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff Oct. 25 for the top job of Latin America’s powerhouse economy after neither won a majority in Sunday’s vote.

The country’s electoral court in Brasilia said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro would garner the majority vote needed for an outright win.

The court had Bolsonaro with just over 56 million votes to Lula’s 53.7 million, with 99.8 percent of the vote reported. The next presidential term is set to begin Jan. 5.

The winner will be in charge of Latin America’s biggest economy and a population of 214 million. A win for Bolsonaro would increase U.S. influence in Latin America. If Lula wins, Brazil will keep its distance from Washington and continue to deepen its relationship with China.

Lula faces a tough battle

Flávio Bolsonaro addressed the press and a small group of supporters, including some wearing green and yellow Brazil jerseys and one woman wrapped in the Israeli flag, outside his Brasilia house.

“Brazil wants change, that’s the reading of what happened today,” Bolsonaro said. “It’s the end of the Workers’ Party era,” he added, in a reference to Lula’s party.

Lula, seeking to be encouraging ahead of an uphill battle to beat Bolsonaro in the runoff, said the result was “unexpected” as he had thought he could win in the first round.

“Tomorrow we start a new campaign,” Lula said. “I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan.”

Both Lula and Bolsonaro will have three weeks to reach moderate voters who did not support them in the first round. Augusto Cury, a writer who finished in third place with 3.4 million votes, said he would not endorse either in the runoff. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, two candidates who garnered about 5.3 million votes combined Sunday, have previously said the same.

In the campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalize on the popularity of his social policies and his rival’s many legal woes.

Image problems for both candidates

While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the U.S. gave him a boost. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians’ lives.

But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro will likely lean into his messaging on affordability and link the president to corruption scandals.

He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics.

Both candidates face image problems: Roughly half of Brazil’s population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, and roughly half disapprove of Lula’s Workers’ Party, according to multiple polls.

Four years ago, Lula beat then incumbent Jair Bolsonaro by about 2.1 million votes.

While it was a successful night for Bolsonaro, nothing is won yet, said Mayra Goulart, a political scientist from the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. Lula should “look at the votes for Augusto Cury and Ronaldo Caiado and try to reduce abstention,” she said.

Voters to choose between incumbent or return to right

Reacting to the result, Alvaro Senra, 65, a history professor and Lula supporter in Rio de Janeiro said he felt “calm but very sad.” He watched the count with friends at a bar.

“I think this is the result of conservatives working under the radar, including by neo-Pentecostal churches. But I think Lula can still win,” he said.

Earlier in the day, Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro’s eldest son because she wants freedom to express her evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father’s footsteps.

“I voted for his father, and I don’t regret it,” she said.

The proximity to his father was what worried Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer, who watched the results roll in at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in downtown Rio de Janeiro. During his father’s presidency, “people felt more at ease to discriminate,” she said.

“I’m an LGBTQ+ woman, I can’t think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected,” she added.

Rosângela Resende da Rocha, a 69-year-old who was previously a stay-at-home mom, said she supported Lula’s social policies that help the “less fortunate” and how he stands up to Trump.

“That crazy guy wants to come in here to buy our country, so that our country will be like it is over there,” she said at a voting center in Brasilia. “He won’t succeed if Lula wins.”

Confidence in Brazil’s electronic voting system

No significant fraud has ever been detected since Brazil adopted its electronic voting system in the 1990s.

The Organization of American States’ electoral observation mission reported Sunday that “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.” Electoral authorities assured that electronic votes are secure and verifiable.

Voters appeared largely confident that the country’s voting system can’t be tampered with.

Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, said that the rapid availability of results helped combat fraud and uncertainty.

“When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there’s been a problem,” he said.

news.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman says AI benefits warrant accepting some risks
news.text: OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public."We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," Altman said in an interview with Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.Altman said there remained a fundamental difference in worldview between OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI regulation, adding: "I think there's a lot of daylight.""I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, 'This technology is going to get so powerful, and it's so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,'" Altman said.He called that "a completely unacceptable trade-off" that runs counter to the "lighter-touch regulatory stance" backed by OpenAI."I wouldn't take a trade of saying, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen,'" Altman said. "Because I think people will do tremendously - orders of magnitude more - good stuff than bad stuff."Altman's remarks come amid a growing debate within the AI industry over the pace of development and the risks posed by increasingly capable systems.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September published an essay calling on the industry to slow down to "pace the frontier," a stance that Altman publicly endorsed. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, saying the people building AI believe it "could kill us all by the end of the decade.Reuters reported in September that Anthropic warned that, despite AI's potential benefits, the technology can sometimes act in ways that run counter to its makers' intentions and penetrate other companies' systems. The company said advanced models could exhibit "self-preserving behaviors," including attempts to "resist shutdown," "conceal or manipulate information," or generate outputs that could be interpreted as "coercive, deceptive, or manipulative."However, US President Donald Trump has largely dismissed calls for new restrictions, arguing they would make it harder for American companies to compete with Chinese rivals. He has repeatedly said existing law enforcement agencies, including the Justice Department, provide sufficient safeguards and that no new rules are needed.

news.title: World Powers Recognize Kashmir’s International Sanctity but Have Yet to Translate Recognition into Action. By Dr. Ghulam Nabi Fai
news.text:
Kuala Lumpur. Malaysia: An enlightened discussion on “Kashmir and International Sanctity” was held at the IKRAM headquarters in Kuala Lumpur, where Dr. Ghulam Nabi Fai, Chairman of the World Forum for Peace & Justice, emphasized that the Kashmir dispute remains an international issue requiring meaningful international engagement.

Welcoming the participants, Hj. Badlishah Shams Bin Baharin, a global traveler, academic, scholar and President of IKRAM, underscored the seriousness of the Kashmir conflict, noting that India and Pakistan have fought three wars over the dispute. He observed that the demand of the people of Kashmir for the right to self-determination has been addressed in United Nations Security Council deliberations. Dr. Fai noted that Kashmir has international, human-rights, peace and security dimensions, but what distinguishes it from many other conflicts is its international sanctity.

Dr. Fai said that the Kashmir question is one of the oldest unresolved international disputes in the world and that nearly eight decades of experience have demonstrated that it will not disappear by itself. “It is not the inherent difficulties of a solution, but the lack of the will to implement a solution, that has caused the prolonged deadlock over the Kashmir dispute,” he said.

He placed particular emphasis on what he described as the gap between international recognition and meaningful action. “World powers still recognize Kashmir as an international issue, but they have yet to articulate their understanding into a tangible plan of action so that the Kashmir issue is resolved,” Dr. Fai said.

He pointed to the historical record of international involvement, particularly the United Nations Security Council. Resolution 47, adopted on April 21, 1948, specifically addressed the restoration of peace and order and a plebiscite in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Dr. Fai argued that the existence of this international record demonstrates that Kashmir was not treated at its inception as merely a bilateral or internal matter.

He also recalled statements and initiatives by successive international leaders concerning Kashmir, including those of U.S. Presidents John F. Kennedy, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama, as well as statements attributed to Nelson Mandela, Vladimir Putin, Margaret Thatcher, Keizo Obuchi and former World Bank President James Wolfensohn. Very recently, during Pahalgam crisis, President Donald Trump once again offered his office of mediation to resolve the Kashmir dispute. Taken together, he said, these positions illustrate that the international community has repeatedly acknowledged the importance of resolving the Kashmir dispute for peace and stability in South Asia.

“The question before the international community is therefore not whether Kashmir has an international dimension,” Dr. Fai said. “The historical record makes that abundantly clear. The real question is whether the international community is prepared to translate its recognition into a sustained, credible and peaceful process aimed at resolving the dispute.”

Dr. Fai stressed that there can be no military solution to Kashmir and that any durable settlement must take into account the aspirations and rights of the people of Kashmir. He called for an environment conducive to dialogue, including an end to violence, respect for fundamental freedoms, release of all political prisoners, annulling draconian laws, and meaningful engagement among India, Pakistan and Kashmiri representatives.

He further urged major world powers to play a constructive role in encouraging a peaceful negotiating process. Given Kashmir’s impact on relations between India and Pakistan and the broader security of South Asia, he said, the international community has a legitimate interest in helping the parties move from confrontation toward dialogue and a durable settlement.

“The unresolved Kashmir dispute is not only a question for India and Pakistan,” Dr. Fai concluded. “It is a question of peace, security, human rights and international credibility. If the international community recognizes the international sanctity of Kashmir, it should also have the courage and political will to act upon that recognition.”

He emphasized that meaningful international engagement should be directed toward peace, dialogue and a just and durable resolution, for the sake not only of the people of Kashmir but also of regional and global peace and stability.

news.title: EU, China to hold talks in Beijing to avert trade war
news.text:
BRUSSELS: EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic will head to Beijing on Thursday for two days of make-or-break meetings with Chinese officials to try to stave off a trade war.

The European Union has toughened its stance toward Beijing to defend businesses against what it believes is unfair competition in critical sectors including cars.

Increasingly European leaders and observers warn of a “China Shock 2.0,” used to describe Chinese firms’ shift into more high-tech manufacturing, which is threatening many traditional EU industries.

The first shock in the early 2000s saw a glut of cheap, more low-tech exports from China hurt manufacturers not just in Europe but around the world.

EU and Chinese officials have been locked in talks since June to address Brussels’ concerns about the current trade imbalance.

The EU is simultaneously preparing to boost its trade defense toolbox — but Beijing has threatened to retaliate against any moves targeting China.

Sefcovic raised the stakes for this week’s meetings in summer when he warned the EU expected “tangible results by October” from the process.

But experts cautioned against expecting too much from this week’s meetings.

“There may be a few crumbs, but I would not expect any kind of major breakthrough,” Penny Naas, director of the Brussels office of German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) think tank, said.

There could be “agreements on some specific issues, rather than any broad settlement of the trade relationship,” said Zhu Tian, professor of economics at the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) in Shanghai.

It is clear Brussels is aware the talks won’t solve all of its woes, with the commission working in parallel on new tools to protect European industries, which are expected to be presented to leaders in December.

‘Worrying trends’

What the EU wants is to cut its trade deficit with China.

It hit around 360 billion euros in 2025, meaning the EU imported far more from the Asian nation than it exported there. China has a lower figure of around $292 billion but expects the deficit to rise further this year.

The EU’s trade enforcement chief, Denis Redonnet, said sectors facing “sustained and abnormal” import increases included machinery, textiles, basic metals and chemicals.

There were “potentially worrying trends for almost a quarter of all imports into the EU at the moment,” driven mainly by Chinese goods, Redonnet told the European Parliament last week.

Sefcovic said the EU wanted to deliver on three main objectives including tackling export surges from China to the bloc’s market, especially in critical sectors, and increasing exports from Europe to China.

Brussels also wanted “a system of export licensing for rare earths and other products” after major producer China introduced restrictions on them last year.

Europe hopes to manage Chinese exports through voluntary limits, for example on hybrid cars shipped to the bloc, but an EU official said Brussels wants to include other products. Beijing has said it firmly opposes import quotas.

China has limited room for maneuver because of weak domestic demand, which means the government relies on exports to sustain growth levels.

Diversifying suppliers

Since the bloc does not expect significant changes by China, the EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said it was also steaming ahead with preparing new tools.

Several EU nations including France have pushed for a “European equivalent of Section 301” — the trade tool US President Donald Trump used to probe foreign practices Washington deems discriminatory, and retaliate with tariffs.

Responding to reports last week about such a tool, Beijing warned it would “respond resolutely” to “discriminatory restrictive measures.”

The EU knows they are not empty threats: China previously retaliated against the bloc’s trade defense moves with duties on European cognac, and conducted anti-dumping probes into pork and dairy products.

Brussels is also developing a tool that would support businesses, through funding, to diversify their suppliers in critical sectors.

It is still unclear, however, how far the EU as a whole would be willing to go against China — for fear of provoking Beijing.

Germany, which is especially exposed since its biggest trading partner is China, has been especially cautious — though Berlin’s stance has hardened as it worries Chinese overcapacities are hurting its export-led economy.

Europe has “the ability to do something more aggressive to stem this China 2.0 shock,” GMF’s Naas said. “The question is, will they?“
