news.title: Iran war may outlast Trump as US weighs options
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 5 (IANS) The Iran conflict could continue through the remainder of President Donald Trump's term and be inherited by his successor, a former senior White House Middle East official warned, as the Trump administration said it was simultaneously pursuing diplomatic and military pressure on Tehran and preparing for further contingencies. Brett McGurk, who served as President Joe Biden's coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa, said he saw no clear path towards a comprehensive settlement with Iran and predicted an extended period of economic pressure, intermittent military exchanges and possible temporary ceasefires. "If I had to make a prediction, this is going to go on through the end of Trump's presidency, and it'll go into -- the next president will have to deal with this chronic problem of Iran that has -- every president has really dealt with this revolutionary system since Jimmy Carter," McGurk told CNN's Fareed Zakaria. "It's been a perennial problem. I've dealt with it now, you know, across administrations," he said. McGurk said the Middle East had undergone a "fundamental" shift in its balance of power since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. He pointed to two subsequent military campaigns involving Iran, including Operation Midnight Hammer against Iranian nuclear infrastructure and the conflict that began on February 28 this year. McGurk said one concern was that the latest conflict began with what he described as an open-ended regime-change objective. "And once you go down that road, you can find yourself very much trapped in kind of how you actually wind it down," he said. McGurk said he could not see an endgame unless Iran's political system fundamentally changed its character and policies or eventually came apart. "But again, that is going to be, I think, way down the road," he said. For now, McGurk predicted a prolonged confrontation. "So, I think we are in this period and it's going to last for some time. Serious economic pressure. You'll have occasional tit-for-tat military exchanges. You might have occasional interim cease fire deals, interim agreements," he said. A comprehensive nuclear settlement appeared even more difficult, McGurk said. He suggested decision-makers in Tehran were likely to view Iran's status as a threshold nuclear state as their ultimate deterrent. "And so, getting that deal on the nuclear side it is going to be really hard," he said. McGurk's assessment came as Energy Secretary Chris Wright said separately that the Trump administration was keeping both military and diplomatic tracks open. Appearing on CBS News' "Face the Nation", Wright was asked about reports that the United States was sending additional defensive equipment to Gulf countries to protect oil infrastructure and that a third carrier strike group was heading to the region. "Look, the president has – has taken a strong stand that Iran, the world's greatest terrorist regime – regime, cannot and will not have nuclear weapons," Wright said. "So, of course, we're looking at every avenue to achieve that goal, economically, to be prepared for what comes militarily." "But we cannot pass to the next administration an Iran armed with nuclear weapons," he said. Asked whether Trump had decided to escalate after Election Day, when the third carrier strike group was expected to arrive, Wright declined to disclose the President's plans. "Oh, I'm definitely not going to get in front of the president's plans or policies," he said. Wright said Trump was "always planning for contingencies and he's always negotiating." Asked whether that meant both diplomatic and military pressure remained active, Wright replied: "Of course, of course, at all times." The conflict is also posing an increasingly difficult energy challenge for the administration. Wright acknowledged there could be no guarantee against another disruption affecting Gulf oil infrastructure. "There's no guarantees. There's no guarantees in conflict. There's no guarantees in life," he said. He nevertheless predicted lower gasoline and diesel prices in the coming weeks, citing increasing supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, record US gasoline production and declining demand after the summer driving season. "Absolutely. Diesel prices have been going down. Gasoline prices have been going down. I expect that to continue," Wright said. Wright said Trump had been aware when making decisions on Iran that they could drive energy prices higher. "If his decisions were political, he would have just kicked the can down the road and delivered a nuclear-armed Iran to the next president," Wright said. news.title: US midterms: 435 House seats, 35 Senate races and $12 billion in spending
news.text:
ReutersElections on November 3 will determine control of Congress, affecting Trump's agenda as he finishes his term.

Washington: Americans go to the polls on November 3 for elections that will shape the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency -- although the president himself will not be on any ballot.The "midterms," held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide control of Congress as well as governorships and thousands of state-level offices.Also Read: US midterm elections: Trump stumps for candidates in deep red Alabama and says he'll be back again next weekA Democratic takeover of either chamber would constrain Trump's agenda and bring greater congressional scrutiny of his administration; Republican victories would preserve the party's control in Washington.Here is a look at the 2026 showdown by the numbers:Live Events- House of Representatives -435: Every seat in the House, the lower chamber of Congress, is contested every two years.218: The magic number for a majority in the 435-seat chamber.3: The net number of seats Democrats need to gain from the 2024 election result to take control. Republicans won a 220-215 majority then, although deaths, resignations and a party switch mean the current House stands at 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies.For Republicans, that means a net loss of two seats is survivable. Three is not.- Senate and the states -35: Senate seats being contested -- 33 in the normal six-year rotation plus special elections in Florida and Ohio.Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage in the 100-seat chamber, counting two independents who vote with the Democrats. Democrats therefore need a net gain of four seats to reach the 51 required for control; a 50-50 tie would be broken by Republican Vice President JD Vance.36: States electing governors, nearly three-quarters of the total.6,139: State legislative seats being regularly contested, across 88 of the country's 99 state legislative chambers.- What the polls say -53-41 percent: The Democratic advantage over Republicans among registered voters asked which party's congressional candidate they would support, in a PBS News/NPR/Marist poll conducted September 14-15.The same survey found Democrats ahead among independent voters by 57 percent to 32 percent.32-41 percent: The range of Trump's approval rating in several major September surveys.Also Read: US midterm elections: 9 key issues that could shape the November pollsReuters/Ipsos put him at 32 percent among US adults, the lowest of his political career, while Marist recorded 39 percent and NBC News 41 percent among registered voters. The surveys use different methodologies and populations, so the figures are not directly comparable -- but none suggests an abundance of presidential coattails.55 percent: Registered voters who told NBC News that Trump's policies had hurt the economy, against 26 percent who said they had helped it.- Money, money, money -About $12 billion: The amount expected to be spent advertising on the 2025-26 election cycle.Ad-tracking company AdImpact forecasts $11.6 billion, exceeding both the previous midterm record of $8.9 billion in 2022 and even the 2024 presidential cycle.Kinetiq Political Insights' latest estimate is slightly higher at $11.96 billion, with a projected range of $11.5 billion to $12.5 billion.$330 million: Advertising spending in the California governor's primary alone, according to AdImpact -- making the preliminary contest to choose November's candidates the most expensive gubernatorial race on record.And that was merely the warm-up.- For the trivia file -2,497: Candidates who ran in US congressional primaries this year, the most in any election cycle since at least 2014. An extraordinary 2,232 of them were chasing House seats.44: House races on November 3 that are rematches between the same major-party candidates who fought for the seat in 2024.Broaden the search to state and local contests and there are 474 electoral rematches nationwide -- proving that in American politics, as in Hollywood, there is rarely any objection to a sequel.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Brazil heads to a runoff election after Bolsonaro and Lula fail to garner a majority of votes
news.text: BRASILIA, Brazil — Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and Brazil's incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff Oct. 25 for the top job of Latin America's powerhouse economy after neither won a majority in Sunday's vote.The country's electoral court in Brasilia said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro would garner the majority vote needed for an outright win.The court had Bolsonaro with just over 56 million votes to Lula's 53.7 million, with 99.8 percent of the vote reported. The next presidential term is set to begin Jan. 5.The winner will be in charge of Latin America's biggest economy and a population of 214 million. A win for Bolsonaro would increase U.S. influence in Latin America. If Lula wins, Brazil will keep its distance from Washington and continue to deepen its relationship with China.Lula faces a tough battleFlávio Bolsonaro addressed the press and a small group of supporters, including some wearing green and yellow Brazil jerseys and one woman wrapped in the Israeli flag, outside his Brasilia house.'Brazil wants change, that's the reading of what happened today,' Bolsonaro said. 'It's the end of the Workers' Party era,' he added, in a reference to Lula's party.Lula, seeking to be encouraging ahead of an uphill battle to beat Bolsonaro in the runoff, said the result was 'unexpected' as he had thought he could win in the first round.'Tomorrow we start a new campaign,' Lula said. 'I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan.'Both Lula and Bolsonaro will have three weeks to reach moderate voters who did not support them in the first round. Augusto Cury, a writer who finished in third place with 3.4 million votes, said he would not endorse either in the runoff. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, two candidates who garnered about 5.3 million votes combined Sunday, have previously said the same.In the campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalize on the popularity of his social policies and his rival's many legal woes.Image problems for both candidatesWhile the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the U.S. gave him a boost. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians' lives.But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro.Bolsonaro will likely lean into his messaging on affordability and link the president to corruption scandals.He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics.Both candidates face image problems: Roughly half of Brazil's population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, and roughly half disapprove of Lula's Workers' Party, according to multiple polls.Four years ago, Lula beat then incumbent Jair Bolsonaro by about 2.1 million votes.While it was a successful night for Bolsonaro, nothing is won yet, said Mayra Goulart, a political scientist from the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. Lula should 'look at the votes for Augusto Cury and Ronaldo Caiado and try to reduce abstention,' she said.Voters to choose between incumbent or return to rightReacting to the result, Alvaro Senra, 65, a history professor and Lula supporter in Rio de Janeiro said he felt 'calm but very sad.' He watched the count with friends at a bar.'I think this is the result of conservatives working under the radar, including by neo-Pentecostal churches. But I think Lula can still win,' he said.Earlier in the day, Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro's eldest son because she wants freedom to express her evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father's footsteps.'I voted for his father, and I don't regret it,' she said.The proximity to his father was what worried Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer, who watched the results roll in at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in downtown Rio de Janeiro. During his father's presidency, 'people felt more at ease to discriminate,' she said.'I'm an LGBTQ+ woman, I can't think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected,' she added.Rosângela Resende da Rocha, a 69-year-old who was previously a stay-at-home mom, said she supported Lula's social policies that help the 'less fortunate' and how he stands up to Trump.'That crazy guy wants to come in here to buy our country, so that our country will be like it is over there,' she said at a voting center in Brasilia. 'He won't succeed if Lula wins.'Confidence in Brazil's electronic voting systemNo significant fraud has ever been detected since Brazil adopted its electronic voting system in the 1990s.The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission reported Sunday that 'the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.' Electoral authorities assured that electronic votes are secure and verifiable.Voters appeared largely confident that the country's voting system can't be tampered with.Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, said that the rapid availability of results helped combat fraud and uncertainty.'When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there's been a problem,' he said.

news.title: How Boeing Design Helped flydubai Plane Despite Losing 32,000 Feet Per Minute
news.text: The aftermath of the near-catastrophic FlyDubai flight that miraculously ended with a safe landing has largely focused on the desperate fight between the two pilots and the heroic effort by passengers and a reserve crew to stabilize the plunging jetliner. But the performance of the aircraft itself also appears to have defied the odds, given the Boeing Co. 737 Max plummeted almost vertically at one point as the two men battled for control of the cockpit. The plane eventually touched down in Saudi Arabia, despite the breakneck maneuvers that seemed to damage some parts of the aircraft, drawing online praise of Boeing's design from US President Donald Trump. Investigators are still working to determine the facts of the incident, but interviews with a test pilot and a review of the plane's design features show the aircraft - and the more than 170 people on board - likely survived thanks to layers of redundancy in aviation and, perhaps, a little luck.Preliminary information indicates that the aircraft dove, climbed rapidly and then dove again after the co-pilot attacked his colleague. Passengers who rushed to the front of the plane were able to stabilize the situation, pulling the attacker off the injured pilot and arresting the airplane's rapid descent that had sent the rest of the cabin into chaos.When the plane touched down in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, unverified images circulating on social media showed a portion of the aircraft's rudder, which controls where the nose of the jet is pointing without rolling the wings, had been torn off.According to FlightRadar24, the aircraft at one point was descending at more than 32,000 feet per minute, a dive whose recovery would've likely seen passengers experience crushing gravitational forces typically stomached by fighter pilots and astronauts. When an aircraft is certified, it is intentionally put in situations that are never expected to occur during normal operations. The Boeing 737 Max involved in the incident is the newest, more efficient iteration of the workhouse single-aisle plane first approved in the 1960s, upgraded with modern engines and avionics."Why do you test out there? The answer is because of the potential for inadvertent exceedances of those limits," said Bob Stoney, a former US Federal Aviation Administration pilot who headed flight testing for several Boeing aircraft including the 737-900ER and led the Max models' return to service after two fatal crashes last decade.The certification process also requires that aircraft go through rigorous ground tests, including intentionally stressing wings to failure.Federal aviation regulations mandate large commercial airliners be tested well beyond their published normal maximum operating limit speed, which for a 737 Max 8 is about 630 miles (1,000 kilometres) per hour, but can change depending on altitude and weather conditions, according to the FAA. The FlyDubai aircraft clocked a maximum speed of about 690 mph during its dive, near the speed of sound at that altitude, according to preliminary data from tracking service FlightRadar24. Damage to any flight control surface like the rudder is typically a critical event that changes how the aircraft flies, potentially endangering all onboard. Stoney said there is a requirement to complete tests for a jammed rudder during certification, but not for the piece to be outright missing. He explained the two cases are relatively aerodynamically similar, as pilots in both situations must fly as if they have lost the rudder entirely. The rudder in a large jet like the 737 is particularly critical during landing, Stoney said, adding that doing so without one in high wind conditions or when the wind is not aligned with the runway is challenging. However, he said the loss of a wing or tail flap would generally be harder to recover from in any situation.The damaged rudder may have been one of many difficult circumstances encountered by the off-duty pilots who happened to be on board the FlyDubai aircraft when the attack took place.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that after being stabbed, the captain managed to unlock the door to the cockpit - which can only be done from inside - to call for help. Passengers intervened, and the off-duty pilots then took control of the airplane."I've been a pilot for 17 years, I've been a captain for the past 11 years, I know what's happening in a flight even with my eyes closed," FlyDubai Captain Smit Machchhar said during a Friday call with Prime Minister Narendra Modi from the hospital. "When I was on the ground, I realized that the aircraft is going down. And I told myself, 'This is the last push, Smit. The door is right there.'" An unforgettable conversation with Captain Smit, filled with pride and emotions. https://t.co/CCf46PKOWR— Narendra Modi (@narendramodi) October 2, 2026In a video released by Netanyahu's office on social media, the passenger who claims to have been first to the cockpit said he grabbed the aircraft controls and pulled them back to arrest the rapid dive after yanking the attacker off the captain. יניב, אתה גיבור אמיתי. אנחנו עם של אריות! https://t.co/55AgmAvzIG— Benjamin Netanyahu - בנימין נתניהו (@netanyahu) September 30, 2026The passenger, identified as Yaniv Hayun, said this was an action he knew to take because he watches the popular Air Crash Investigation television series on National Geographic.The Boeing 737 has two central steering yokes shaped like horns to maneuver the plane, unlike an Airbus SE A320, which is flown using control sticks positioned off to the side of each pilot's seat - and which might have been less intuitive to manipulate for an amateur.Throughout aviation history, there are examples of accidents where layers of safety and redundancy helped avert tragedy, but also plenty where seemingly miraculous circumstances were the difference between a safe outcome and a disaster.Perhaps most famous was the 2009 accident dubbed "the miracle on the Hudson," when a US Airways Airbus A320 landed on the Hudson River following an extremely rare dual engine failure upon ingesting a flock of birds. All 155 people on board survived."Consequently, this accident has been portrayed as a 'successful' ditching," the US National Transportation Safety Board said in its final report at the time."However, the investigation revealed that the success of this ditching mostly resulted from a series of fortuitous circumstances," namely that the pilot had nearly 20,000 flight hours, the plane was equipped with extra slides and life rafts, and the ditching took place in an area close to large boats that immediately came to the rescue, the report said.As if to warn the industry to remain vigilant despite the positive outcome, the report added: "The investigation revealed several areas where safety improvements are needed."(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: EU, China to hold Beijing talks this week to avert trade war
news.text:
IANSEU trade chief Maros Sefcovic is set to visit Beijing for crucial discussions regarding trade relations

EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic will head to Beijing on Thursday for two days of make-or-break meetings with Chinese officials to try to stave off a trade war.The European Union has toughened its stance towards Beijing to defend businesses against what it believes is unfair competition in critical sectors including cars.Increasingly European leaders and observers warn of a "China Shock 2.0", used to describe Chinese firms' shift into more high-tech manufacturing, which is threatening many traditional EU industries.The first shock in the early 2000s saw a glut of cheap, more low-tech exports from China hurt manufacturers not just in Europe but around the world.EU and Chinese officials have been locked in talks since June to address Brussels' concerns about the current trade imbalance.Live EventsThe EU is simultaneously preparing to boost its trade defence toolbox -- but Beijing has threatened to retaliate against any moves targeting China.Sefcovic raised the stakes for this week's meetings in summer when he warned the EU expected "tangible results by October" from the process.But experts cautioned against expecting too much from this week's meetings."There may be a few crumbs, but I would not expect any kind of major breakthrough," Penny Naas, director of the Brussels office of German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) think tank, said.There could be "agreements on some specific issues, rather than any broad settlement of the trade relationship", said Zhu Tian, professor of economics at the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) in Shanghai.It is clear Brussels is aware the talks won't solve all of its woes, with the commission working in parallel on new tools to protect European industries, which are expected to be presented to leaders in December.'Worrying trends' What the EU wants is to cut its trade deficit with China.It hit around 360 billion euros in 2025, meaning the EU imported far more from the Asian nation than it exported there. China has a lower figure of around $292 billion but expects the deficit to rise further this year.The EU's trade enforcement chief, Denis Redonnet, said sectors facing "sustained and abnormal" import increases included machinery, textiles, basic metals and chemicals.There were "potentially worrying trends for almost a quarter of all imports into the EU at the moment", driven mainly by Chinese goods, Redonnet told the European Parliament last week.Sefcovic said the EU wanted to deliver on three main objectives including tackling export surges from China to the bloc's market, especially in critical sectors, and increasing exports from Europe to China.Brussels also wanted "a system of export licensing for rare earths and other products" after major producer China introduced restrictions on them last year.Europe hopes to manage Chinese exports through voluntary limits, for example on hybrid cars shipped to the bloc, but an EU official said Brussels wants to include other products. Beijing has said it firmly opposes import quotas.China has limited room for manoeuvre because of weak domestic demand, which means the government relies on exports to sustain growth levels.Diversifying suppliers Since the bloc does not expect significant changes by China, the EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said it was also steaming ahead with preparing new tools.Several EU nations including France have pushed for a "European equivalent of Section 301" -- the trade tool US President Donald Trump used to probe foreign practices Washington deems discriminatory, and retaliate with tariffs.Responding to reports last week about such a tool, Beijing warned it would "respond resolutely" to "discriminatory restrictive measures".The EU knows they are not empty threats: China previously retaliated against the bloc's trade defence moves with duties on European cognac, and conducted anti-dumping probes into pork and dairy products.Brussels is also developing a tool that would support businesses, through funding, to diversify their suppliers in critical sectors.It is still unclear, however, how far the EU as a whole would be willing to go against China -- for fear of provoking Beijing.Germany, which is especially exposed since its biggest trading partner is China, has been especially cautious -- though Berlin's stance has hardened as it worries Chinese overcapacities are hurting its export-led economy.Europe has "the ability to do something more aggressive to stem this China 2.0 shock", GMF's Naas said. "The question is, will they?"Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: 'Out with a bang': Donald Trump won't be quiet lame-duck president
news.text:
‘Kingmaker’

U.S. presidents are often punished in midterm elections, weakening their party in Congress and leaving them with the dreaded lame-duck epithet as their power wanes toward the end.

But if Republicans lose the House of Representatives as expected — and possibly the Senate, too — Trump will find himself in a peculiarly precarious position as Democrats probe alleged corruption or abuse of power.

Trump has already signalled he will take his usual combative approach.

“They’ll probably go after me and I’ll go after them,” Trump said in a Time magazine interview published this week.

“I think he’s going to be in attack mode,” Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution told AFP.

First of all, Trump baselessly disputed his 2020 presidential election loss to Joe Biden and it is “entirely possible” he could claim irregularities in the midterms as well, said Hass.

Then, Trump could direct the U.S. Department of Justice to investigate leading Democrats probing him in the same way that a number of his opponents have found themselves facing legal action.

news.title: Elon Musk’s heartbroken baby mama Shivon Zilis reveals billionaire has ended their relationship with no warning…’I’ve loved him more than life itself’
news.text:
By DANA KENNEDY, SENIOR INVESTIGATIVE REPORTER and EMILY CRANE 17:02 02 Oct 2026, updated 09:11 03 Oct 2026

Elon Musk’s longtime love and baby mama Shivon Zilis has revealed the billionaire abruptly ended their relationship ‘with no warning’ – with the mom-of-four declaring ‘it’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week.’

‘Hurting’ Zilis, an executive at Musk’s brain implant startup Neuralink, poured her heart out in a lengthy X post on Friday – just hours after eagle-eyed social media users noticed the billionaire had stopped following her on the platform he owns.

‘I’ve loved him more than life itself and he’s taught me 100 lifetimes of knowledge and made my cup overflow with life meaning, so there is a lot of loss, but luckily we created four beautiful little loves of my life,’ Zilis, 40, wrote on X.

‘I am so beyond grateful for our children and they make every single day the best day of my life! I do hope and pray he and I can be great friends and coparents.’

Zilis, who is believed to have first embarked on a secret tryst with the Space X founder back in 2016, went on to describe Musk as a ‘tortured soul.’

‘I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,’ she wrote.

‘I loved being that counterbalancing place of safety, sense of calm, and love – and delighted in bringing a smile back to his face when he was down. I will miss him dearly.’

Zilis – the mother of four of Musk’s 14 kids – hinted, too, that she was blindsided by the breakup – sharing a screenshot of loved-up text messages the pair had exchanged just last week.

‘It was really wonderful to see you for breakfast. Love you very much,’ Zilis texted Musk.

‘Love you too. I didn’t realize that this Xi dinner included significant other (Beijing one did not) or I would have invited you,’ he responded on September 24, referencing the White House state dinner for the Chinese president. Zilis replied: ‘Aw, that means so much to me. Thank you.’

Musk, 55, hasn’t yet commented on the breakup.

Zilis ended her post by saying: ‘I’m hurting, but care deeply about E and will always be cheering for his happiness. God speed, Elon, the world is lucky to have you.’

The first apparent sign of trouble in the couple’s romance came back on September 28 when Zilis had posted a cryptic message on social media: ‘New day, new life.’

Then, earlier on Friday, Big Tech Alert, an account that tracks the online activity of technology figures, flagged that Musk had unfollowed her.

The Tesla founder only follows around 1,400 accounts.

News of the shock split comes just months after Zilis – who is one of four women Musk has children with – took the stand as a key witness in the Space X founder’s case against OpenAI earlier this year.

It was during her testimony that key details about their once-secret romance were laid bare.

Zilis, who was born in Ontario, Canada and studied at Yale University, had first met Musk through OpenAI – the artificial intelligence lab he co-founded in 2015.

She testified that their relationship began as ‘a one-off’ at a corporate off-site event – but later turned romantic around 2016.

Zilis told the jury that when she decided to have children as a single mom, Musk ‘offered to make a donation’ as a platonic sperm donor towards the end of 2020.

Their twins, Strider and Azure, were born by IVF in November 2021. News of their third child, Arcadia, surfaced in June 2024. And their son, Seldon Lycurgus, followed in February 2025.

Zilis testified that she lives in a house in Austin, Texas where Musk often stays when he visits their children.

Musk, for his part, called Zilis his ‘partner’ when it was his turn to testify.

The couple were spotted holding hands as they arrived at the wedding of White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino at President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate back in February.

Prior to becoming director of operations and special projects at Neuralink, Zilis had previously worked as a project director on Tesla’s Autopilot team from 2017 to 2019.

In the wake of their split, it wasn’t immediately clear whether Zilis would keep her roles at Neuralink and Musk’s other companies.

The Daily Mail has reached out to Zilis and Musk.

news.title: Nobel 2026: Ozempic, Mounjaro research tipped for medicine prize
news.text:
APThe 2026 Nobel season is set to reveal the winners of various prestigious awards, starting with medicine

Stockholm: Research into hormones that regulate appetite is on everybody's lips for the Nobel medicine prize, to be announced on Monday when the 2026 Nobel season kicks off.The winners of the six Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics will be revealed daily from October 5-12.Monday's medicine prize, to be announced at 11:30 am (0930 GMT), could go to research that paved the way for weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, Nobel watchers told AFP.That could include microbiome research, the discovery of the leptin and ghrelin hormones regulating satiety and hunger, and research into a hormone released by the intestine after we eat which signals satiety, called "glucagon-like peptide 1" (GLP-1), which drugs like Ozempic mimic."A Nobel Prize recognising any of that work is a likelihood," said David Pendlebury, who heads research analysis at data analytics firm Clarivate, which predicts potential Nobel winners based on the number of citations of their work.Live Events"I would put GLP-1 at the top of the list, just because of its enormous worldwide clinical impact," he said.Many scientists have made significant contributions in the field, though three regularly mentioned for the Nobel are Canadian endocrinologist Daniel Drucker, Danish physician Jens Juul Holst and Yugoslav-born American chemist Svetlana Mojsov.Skin science or immunology? If the Nobel committee were to go in another direction, stem cell research into how skin regenerates and heals wounds could get the nod, with American cell biologist Elaine Fuchs and her British colleague Fiona Watt recognised as leaders in the field, according to Annika Ostman, science reporter at Swedish public broadcaster SR.The honour could also go to a new imaging technique, called optical coherence tomography.The non-invasive technique uses reflected light to create high-resolution, cross-sectional images of biological tissues, particularly the retina and optic nerve, allowing doctors to detect and monitor disease.Yet another field that may have caught the medicine committee's eye is that of adhesion receptors in the immune system, identified by US immunologist Timothy Springer.These receptors are molecular grips on immune cells that help them stick to blood vessels, enter tissues, and reach infections.They are crucial for directing the body's immune defences and are targets for research into treatments of several inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.Research into breast cancer or DNA sequencing that helped combat coronavirus could also be honoured.The medicine prize will be followed by the prizes for physics on Tuesday and chemistry on Wednesday.The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, with some pundits suggesting that the Swedish Academy could follow up last year's award to Hungary's Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Latin America.Argentine author Samanta Schweblin, 48, could be one such pick, literary critic Lina Kalmteg told AFP.Others often mentioned in Nobel speculation include Antiguan-American author Jamaica Kincaid, Chinese writer Can Xue, Australia's Gerald Murnane and Alexis Wright, Thomas Pynchon of the US and Mexican writer Cristina Rivera Garza.All eyes on peace Perhaps the most keenly anticipated award is that due on Friday, the peace prize -- the only Nobel to be awarded in Oslo.This year, some experts have suggested the jury could choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, after last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, stirred controversy.US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively last year to get the prize -- Machado ended up giving him her Nobel medal -- and the committee is aware he will be watching closely again."There's always a lot of lobbying, and ultimately perhaps also attempts to exert pressure on the committee," the secretary of the Nobel committee, Kristian Berg Harpviken, told AFP in an interview."We're very used to that."Among possible laureates this year are a joint prize to Save the Children and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children's rights activist campaigning for the return of Ukrainian children illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories.Others include Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) after the deadliest year on record for the profession in 2025.The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October news.title: Africa faces gunboat diplomacy without the gunboats
news.text:
“Speak softly and carry a big stick; you will go far.” That was one of the mantras of Theodore ‘Teddy’ Roosevelt, the 26th president of the United States. It meant diplomacy backed by force. As US imperial ambitions expanded, the message was clear: negotiations carried more weight when the other party knew what refusal might cost.

But there is another ‘diplomatic’ practice from a few decades before Teddy, one associated with the British Royal Navy in the nineteenth century and demonstrated by American Commodore Matthew Perry’s arrival in Japan with warships in 1853. Perry came to secure access. His ships made the consequences of resistance unmistakable.

For Africa, the vessels have changed. The question of who gets to dictate the terms remains.

US president Donald Trump is not renowned for speaking softly. His administration’s restrictions on entry to the United States have affected countries across the continent. Washington’s June 2025 proclamation imposed full entry restrictions on nationals of seven African countries, including Chad, the Republic of the Congo and Sudan. A December expansion added further African countries, including Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, while imposing partial restrictions on others, including Nigeria, Senegal and Tanzania. These measures contain exceptions, but their continental reach is clear.

Washington presents these broader restrictions as responses to security concerns, inadequate screening and visa overstays. They differ from sanctions aimed at particular officials over disputed government policies. Yet both demonstrate the power that comes with controlling access.

Who may enter? On whose terms? And what must a government change to keep the door open?

South Africa offers a revealing case study. On 15 September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions targeting people involved in policies Washington says enable uncompensated land seizures, racial discrimination or the incitement of violence against minority groups. No individuals were named.

Prof. Piet Croucamp, political analyst from the North-West University (NWU), says the ambiguity makes the restrictions an instrument of political leverage.

“The most striking thing about the statement is how vague it is. It names no individuals and relies on a provision that gives US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wide discretion to bar people whose entry is deemed harmful to US foreign policy interests. That leaves Washington room to target anyone from legislators to bureaucrats and other officials. Julius Malema may be a principal target.”

That is his assessment of the South African dispute. Its implications deserve attention beyond Pretoria.

“In practice, the visa restrictions are less a precise legal instrument than a flexible political stick that can be used selectively. They mark another step in the Trump administration’s deterioration of relations with South Africa.”

A flexible stick is useful precisely because those facing it cannot be certain where it will land next.

For African governments, the concern is therefore bigger than whether a minister can board a flight to Washington. It is whether access to a powerful country becomes conditional on accepting its interpretation of domestic policy, its diplomatic priorities and its preferred partnerships.

South Africa’s dispute illustrates how quickly these questions overlap. Washington has also criticised Pretoria’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice. A disagreement over domestic legislation consequently sits alongside a confrontation over foreign policy.

None of this places African governments beyond criticism. Sovereignty does not excuse corruption, repression or policies that fail their own citizens. Nor does a government become principled merely by opposing Washington.

Croucamp makes that distinction when assessing Pretoria.

“There is a fair argument that South Africa’s foreign policy is driven less by consistent human rights principles than by ideology and the ANC’s historical relationships. It is a complicated picture.”

It is. But acknowledging a government’s inconsistencies does not give another government an unlimited mandate to determine its choices.

The nineteenth-century gunboat carried power because its guns did not necessarily have to be fired. Its presence demonstrated what could happen if demands were ignored. Visas, tariffs, financial restrictions and access to markets can carry a similar threat.

These instruments differ in purpose and effect. A visa restriction on an official is not equivalent to a tariff affecting an entire industry. That difference is precisely why escalation matters.

Croucamp’s warning concerns South Africa, but the underlying vulnerability is familiar wherever livelihoods depend on decisions made in distant capitals.

“The larger risk is that targeting individuals through visa restrictions makes it easier to escalate to trade measures. Changes to AGOA access or tariffs would hurt far more South Africans than a visa ban. That wider relationship matters more than the visa restrictions alone.”

When pressure moves from officials to economic relationships, the people paying the price may have had little influence over the dispute. Workers, exporters and their families become exposed to a confrontation conducted in the language of national interests.

Africa’s answer cannot end with indignation. Nor can it depend on exchanging reliance on Washington for reliance on another powerful capital.

Greater room to make independent choices requires stronger economies, more trading partners and more trade within Africa. The African Continental Free Trade Area aims to create a single market for goods and services and deepen the continent’s economic integration. Making that ambition work would also strengthen Africa’s ability to negotiate.

That requires functioning infrastructure, credible institutions and governments willing to remove obstacles between African businesses. Sovereignty needs practical foundations. A country with few economic alternatives has less room to resist pressure, however forcefully its leaders speak.

Africa is a continent of different states, interests and vulnerabilities. A common response need not mean agreement on every dispute. It should mean recognising the danger of allowing external powers to negotiate with each country from a position of overwhelming dependence.

The gunboats have not disappeared from international politics. But they are no longer required at every harbour. Sometimes a visa restriction delivers the warning. Sometimes access to a market supplies the ammunition.

South Africa is facing that warning now. The rest of Africa should be paying attention to the bigger sticks still within Washington’s reach.

By Bertie Jacobs

news.title: Poll: Americans Blame Trump for Higher Prices, Cost of Living
news.text:
A poll shows that a majority of Americans blame President Donald Trump for rising prices and higher costs of living as the midterm election approaches.

Surveying 2,140 potential voters nationwide between September 24 and 28 with a margin of error of +/-2.9 percentage points, the poll from the Associated Press (AP)-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17 percent of Americans approve of the president’s handling of higher prices while only 26 percent approve of his handling of the economy overall. Roughly 65 percent of those polled blamed high prices on the president’s policies.

When broken down along party lines, 67 percent of Republicans said higher prices were the result of factors beyond the president’s control. In 2022, the same poll showed that roughly 87 percent of Democrats said that higher prices were beyond President Joe Biden’s control while 44 percent of the broader public believed higher prices were the result of Biden’s policies.

“Trump is also falling short of expectations on the cost of living, with 69 percent of the public saying his handling of the issue has been worse than expected, including 52 percent of Republicans,” noted the poll.

“More than half of adults say the country as a whole, the national economy, and their local economy are worse off since Trump was reelected in 2025,” it continued. “Forty-six percent say they and their families are worse off since the start of Trump’s second administration. Most Americans (73 percent) say the country is heading in the wrong direction, including 92 percent of Democrats and 47 percent of Republicans.”

The poll also showed that the president is faring no better with Americans on his handling of trade and foreign policy, with 68 percent disapproving of his trade negotiations with other countries and 64 percent saying his tariff policy went too far.

The president fared slightly better on the issue of immigration with a 39 percent approval rating.

“About half (48 percent) say his handling of immigration has gone worse than expected, another quarter (23 percent) feel that it has gone better than expected,” the study added.

The poll also showed that 71 percent of Americans disapprove of the president’s handling of Iran, with 69 percent of those polled saying that they do not consider the war worth fighting.

Approval ratings for the president as the midterms loom have ranged from as high as 39 percent to as low as 29 percent. According to Fox News, Republican performance in the coming midterms will hinge on several factors, most specifically inflation and base enthusiasm.

A poll shows that a majority of Americans blame President Donald Trump for rising prices and higher costs of living as the midterm election approaches.

news.title: Brazil’s presidential election between Bolsonaro, Lulu heads to runoff after both fail to garner a majority of votes
news.text:
BRASILIA, Brazil (AP) — Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and Brazil’s incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff Oct. 25 for the top job of Latin America’s powerhouse economy after neither won a majority in Sunday’s vote.

The country’s electoral court in Brasilia said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro would garner the majority vote needed for an outright win.

The court had Bolsonaro with just over 55.8 million votes to Lula’s nearly 53.2 million. Both candidates were poised to address supporters.

The next presidential term is set to begin Jan. 5, 2027.

The winner will be in charge of Latin America’s biggest economy and a population of 214 million. A win for Bolsonaro would increase U.S. influence in Latin America. If Lula wins, Brazil will keep its distance from Washington and continue to deepen its relationship with China.

Lula faces a tough battle

Both Lula and Bolsonaro will have three weeks to reach moderate voters who did not support them in the first round. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, two candidates who garnered about 5.3 million votes combined Sunday, have previously said they will not endorse either in the runoff.

In the campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalize on the popularity of his social policies and his rival’s many legal woes.

While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the U.S. gave him a boost. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians’ lives.

But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro will likely lean into his messaging on affordability and link the president to corruption scandals.

He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics.

“Brazil needs change. Brazil can’t stand so much suffering,” he told reporters at the Rio de Janeiro voting center where he cast his vote Sunday.

Both candidates face image problems: Roughly half of Brazil’s population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, and roughly half disapprove of Lula’s Workers Party, according to multiple polls.

Four years ago, Lula beat then incumbent Jair Bolsonaro by about 2.1 million votes.

Voters choose between incumbent or return to right

“I’m feeling calm but very sad with the result,” said Alvaro Senra, 65, a history professor and Lula supporter in Rio de Janeiro who watched the count with friends at a bar. “I think this is the result of conservatives working under the radar, including by neo-Pentecostal churches. But I think Lula can still win.”

Earlier in the day, Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro’s eldest son because she wants freedom to express her evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father’s footsteps.

“I voted for his father, and I don’t regret it,” she said.

The proximity to his father was what worried Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer, who watched the results roll in at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in downtown Rio de Janeiro. During his father’s presidency, “people felt more at ease to discriminate,” she said.

“I’m an LGBTQ+ woman, I can’t think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected,” she added.

Rosângela Resende da Rocha, a 69-year-old who was previously a stay-at-home mom, said she supported Lula’s social policies that help the “less fortunate” and how he stands up to Trump.

“That crazy guy wants to come in here to buy our country, so that our country will be like it is over there,” she said at a voting center in Brasilia. “He won’t succeed if Lula wins.”

Confidence in Brazil’s electronic voting system

No significant fraud has ever been detected since Brazil adopted its electronic voting system in the 1990s.

The Organization of American States’ electoral observation mission reported Sunday that “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.” Electoral authorities have assured that electronic votes are secure and verifiable.

Voters appeared largely confident that the country’s voting system can’t be tampered with.

Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, said that the rapid availability of results helped combat fraud and uncertainty.

“When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there’s been a problem,” he said.

news.title: Can Trump Win Nobel Peace Prize 2026? What Experts Said
news.text: US President Donald Trump will not win this year's Nobel Peace Prize as he wages war with Iran, but his influence will still be felt by the awarding body that picks the laureate, according to experts.Last year's award, to Venezuela's Maria Corina Machado, was unique in the prize's 125-year history, coming amid repeated lobbying by Trump to get the award. Weeks later, Machado gave her gold Nobel medal to Trump, in a bid to win support for her efforts for a democratic Venezuela.This year, the five-strong body will be mindful of picking someone who can withstand pressure from Trump, according to Haakon Gjerloew, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo."I think last year's events around the Nobel Peace Prize, Maria Corina Machado giving it to Trump afterwards, will affect some of the considerations that they make," he told Reuters."One worry the committee might have is whether awarding it to someone could put them under pressure from Donald Trump ... I think the committee will consider whether the award does more harm than good."That could mean an award to Pope Leo, the International Criminal Court, the International Court of Justice or Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, experts say. The announcement is on October 9.Leo, the first US-born pope, has said he would continue to speak out against war, after the president called him "weak" for criticising the US conflict with Iran. The Pope's encyclical on AI, his advocacy for dialogue and the peaceful resolution of conflicts, his calls for respect for migrants and his humanitarian work could justify a prize."The Pope stands (for) more than just as a religious figure. He has emerged as a leading thought leader," Karim Haggag, director of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told Reuters.Italy's Albanese, meanwhile, has been under fire from the US and Israel for her criticism of Israel's conduct of its war against Hamas in Gaza and the occupation of the West Bank.SAFE CHOICE INSTEAD? To be sure, last year's shock events could have the opposite effect on the committee: go for a safe, uncontroversial choice less likely to antagonise Trump, who blamed Norway, where the award is decided, for not giving him the accolade last time.That could mean recognising Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, a Sudanese network of community groups providing aid during the civil war, or non-governmental group Save the Children for helping children in conflicts.But the committee is also under scrutiny to address Trump's challenges to the international order the committee cherishes, said Oeivind Stenersen, a historian who has written about the Nobel Peace Prize."They have a certain pressure ... to be tough against Trump," he told Reuters. "In this serious international situation, this year calls for a Peace Prize in defence of liberal democracy, international law and human rights."This could mean honouring the ICC at a time when Washington is preparing sweeping sanctions against the global tribunal, according to sources, while an award to the ICJ would support respecting the sovereignty of nation-states and resolving disputes peacefully.Trump has reportedly been nominated by the leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan, but his chances were "quite low", according to Gjerloew.Trump's pressure on the Norwegian Nobel Committee has stunned many, including Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa, a Filipino and American journalist, who said she watched last year with "horror". "Bullies don't run the world," she told Reuters during a visit to Oslo in September. "There are standards we live by. Might doesn't make it right."(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Last year's Nobel Peace Prize award, to Venezuela's Maria Corina Machado, was unique in the 125-year history, coming amid repeated lobbying by Donald Trump to get the award.

news.title: US withdraws all bomber planes from UK airbase — Pentagon
news.text: WASHINGTON, United States — The Pentagon confirmed reports Sunday that the United States has withdrawn all B-1 bomber planes from Royal Air Force Fairford, the UK airbase where a suspicious news.title: ‘Out with a bang’: Trump won’t be a quiet lame duck
news.text:
Published: 21:05 EDT, 4 October 2026 | Updated: 21:05 EDT, 4 October 2026

US President Donald Trump will have just over two years left in power after the midterms

What’s more volatile than President Donald Trump? The answer may be a lame duck Donald Trump after the US midterm elections.

The 80-year-old billionaire faces a bruising final two years in the White House if Republicans lose control of Congress in the November 3 polls amid voter anger over the Iran war and soaring prices.

Investigations and a possible third impeachment would loom as his Democratic foes seek revenge. The president who loves to boast of his power would find much of it stymied.

But Trump with his back to the wall could cause major upheaval, from revenge at home to wars abroad — and influencing the race to be his successor in 2028.

“I don’t think he is going to go out with a whimper, he’s going to try to go out with a bang,” said Allan Lichtman, a professor at American University and author of “Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation.”

“He can’t stand not being the center of attention. So this may spark him to be even more aggressive,” Lichtman told AFP.

US presidents are often punished in midterm elections, weakening their party in Congress and leaving them with the dreaded lame duck epithet as their power wanes towards the end.

US President Donald Trump is likely to face fresh investigations if Republicans lose control of Congress in the midterms

But if Republicans lose the House of Representatives as expected — and possibly the Senate too — Trump will find himself in a peculiarly precarious position as Democrats probe alleged corruption or abuse of power.

Trump has already signaled he will take his usual combative approach.

“They’ll probably go after me, and I’ll go after them,” Trump said in a Time Magazine interview published this week.

“I think he’s going to be in attack mode,” Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution told AFP.

First of all, Trump baselessly disputed his 2020 presidential election loss to Joe Biden and it is “entirely possible” he could claim irregularities in the midterms as well, said Hass.

Then, Trump could direct the US Department of Justice to investigate leading Democrats probing him, in the same way that a number of his opponents have found themselves facing legal action.

In the longer term, Trump sometimes hints at running for a constitutionally-barred third term in the White House, even wearing a “Trump 2028” hat at a gala media dinner in July.

Lichtman said talk of a third term was to “stay relevant” but added that Trump would certainly “keep the focus on himself by being the kingmaker” for the Republican nomination.

Trump — who hosted the television show “The Apprentice” in which he famously uttered the catchphrase “you’re fired” — has been notably coy about backing either Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio for the top job.

“I assume he’ll want to keep the suspense,” said Hass. “Who’s going to watch the show if it’s already been predetermined who’s the winner?”

Outgoing US presidents have often doubled down on foreign policy in the waning days of their terms, as it’s the area in which they have the most power.

US President Donald Trump may retreat into his White House building projects, like the new South Lawn helipad

Trump recently said he may resume bombing Iran after the midterms, but prolonging a quagmire that his MAGA base hates could be politically and militarily risky.

“You could make the argument that he’ll let it rip, but I don’t think he wants his legacy to be a warmonger. He wants his legacy to have left America stronger,” said Hass, who served in the National Security Council under president Barack Obama.

Hass expected Trump to continue the US pullback from some of its western allies while maintaining detente with authoritarian Russia and China and keeping a focus on Latin America.

On trade however, Trump would likely remain “unrelentingly active,” as shown by his recent hostility towards Canada, Hass said.

Trump, like many other soon-to-be retirees, ultimately may be more interested in a little home improvement.

The real estate tycoon appears increasingly obsessed by his construction projects at the White House, such as his new ballroom and helipad.

For Trump, stamping his mark on Washington in granite and concrete may be the greatest legacy of all.

“I love doing it,” Trump said during a recent event at the White House, “because that’s what I did my whole life.”

news.title: Trump names U.S. intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new AI czar
news.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday he had named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, as the administration's artificial intelligence czar, tasking him with co-ordinating the government's efforts to maintain U.S. leadership in the technology.

Trump, who has pushed ​to rename AI as "super intelligence," said Clayton would head ​the newly created "Super Intelligence Force" (SIF), overseeing the government's engagement with consumers, religious groups, AI companies and other stakeholders.

In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump wrote ​that SIF would aim to "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super ⁠Intelligence" and to "protect the interests, ⁠and improve the lives, of all Americans."

How AI could usher in a 'new scientific golden age' — if it doesn't kill us all firstVideoTrump praises AI companies for self-policing plan, but critics want more oversight

The announcement ‌confirmed a Wall Street Journal report in which Clayton, appointed national intelligence chief in August, said Trump had tapped him to lead the administration's push to keep the United States at the forefront of AI.

"The risk of not being first is high," Clayton told the newspaper.

Clayton said ⁠the task force would have 120 days to produce a report assessing the risks and opportunities posed by AI and recommending what role the federal government should play.

AI safety concerns

The safety of AI has become a major issue ‌in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade. Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action.

Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive ​oversight could weaken competitiveness against China. He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on ⁠governing AI technology.

Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, ⁠and recommend ways to strengthen federal response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task ⁠force's charter.

This ⁠is the second time Trump has ​named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar ​role at the beginning of Trump's ⁠second term.

In addition to Clayton, the task force's leaders will include Andrew Ferguson, Federal Trade Commission chair; Pentagon chief technology officer Emil Michael; and Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management, Trump wrote.

The panel will report to the president and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, he said.

news.title: Bolsonaro Edges Lula, Sending Brazil’s Presidential Election to Runoff
news.text:
Brazil’s presidential race has been jolted by an unexpected first-round result: Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of far-right former leader Jair Bolsonaro, edged ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, sending the contest to a run-off in three weeks.

Defying opinion polls that had put Mr Lula in front, Flavio Bolsonaro took about 47% of the vote, while the incumbent secured 45%.

If Mr Bolsonaro prevails in the 25 October election, Brazil would become the latest Latin American country to tilt to the right — a regional shift championed by US President Donald Trump.

Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva addresses supporters in Sao Paulo

The vote also delivered a string of important parliamentary gains for the right, compounding the challenge for Mr Lula, who at 80 is pursuing a fourth term in a bid to cement his political legacy.

Framing the stakes in stark terms, Mr Lula cast the contest as a fight between democracy and “barbarism” and told voters Brazil’s sovereignty was under threat amid pressure from the United States.

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, had maintained a relatively low profile nationally until receiving the backing of his jailed father, and had not previously signalled plans to seek the presidency.

Mr Lula called his first-round stumble “unexpected”, but promised a stronger campaign heading into the decisive vote in three weeks.

“I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people,” the 80-year-old said. 

Bolsonaro dynasty

During the campaign, it emerged that Flavio Bolsonaro was under investigation for corruption linked to the financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father.

The project was bankrolled by jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro, who is under investigation in connection with a financial scandal.

For many voters, the revelations appeared to make little difference.

“Things are truly terrible. As far as I’m concerned, the left just doesn’t work anymore,” said tech worker Joao Batista, 36, saying he was frustrated by the “horrible” cost of basic goods.

Flavio Bolsonaro speaks to supporters in Brasilia

The probe also triggered a rare public clash in the Supreme Court — a confrontation experts said hurt Mr Lula’s campaign.

Even so, some Brazilians expressed little enthusiasm for another election dominated by familiar names.

Oscarina de Oliveira, a 62-year-old caregiver, said she had intended to vote for Mr Lula, as she always has. But “when I got there, I switched to Bolsonaro. Just to see what happens, to see if anything changes.”

The election signalled a resurgence for the Bolsonaro family after Jair Bolsonaro lost his re-election bid in 2022, a defeat that was followed by violent riots in the capital and his conviction last year for attempting a coup.

Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro and another one of Jair Bolsonaro’s sons, Carlos Bolsonaro, both won seats in the Senate.

Jair Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan, 28, was elected as a federal politician.

Trump watches on

Mr Trump said he was watching the election “very closely”, though he stopped short of endorsing Flavio Bolsonaro.

The US president has used tariffs and sanctions to pressure Brasilia over complaints that include the trial of his ally Jair Bolsonaro and allegations of unfair trade practices.

Mr Lula repeatedly warned Mr Trump not to “meddle” in the elections.

He also pledged that Brazil would keep control over developing its vast rare-earth reserves, resources that have drawn attention from Washington and other foreign powers.

Some supporters of Mr Lula followed the results in Cinelandia square in downtown Rio de Janeiro

“I support Lula because he stands up for the poor. Flavio will sell our Brazil off to foreigners,” said Victor Jorge Martins, a 25-year-old event planner.

Flavio Bolsonaro has argued Brazil could be a “solution” to reduce US reliance on China for critical minerals.

Climate change absent

Widely praised for social welfare programmes that lifted millions out of poverty, Mr Lula returned to office in the 2022 elections after serving time in prison on a corruption conviction later overturned on procedural grounds.

In his third term, inflation and unemployment fell. Still, many voters say the cost of living remains too high.

Mr Lula has also moved aggressively to curb deforestation in the Amazon, while supporting oil exploration.

Despite an increasing number of extreme weather events across Brazil, climate change has largely been missing from the campaign debate.

“It is important to elect a candidate who defends our territory, who defends nature,” said Tainara da Costa Cruz, 22, who lives on the banks of the Rio Negro in Amazonas state and voted for Mr Lula.

FBI Director Kash Patel is engaged to his country singer girlfriend, Alexis Wilkins, the pair announced in a post to X on Sunday evening.

Wilkins, 27, posted a black-and-white photo of herself standing with Patel, 46, flashing her hand in front of them to show off her ring with the caption, “Went and got the law involved.” The two have been dating since before Patel took over as head of the FBI in 2025, when she attended his swearing in.

The country singer and political commentator released her debut album in 2023. Wilkins has been affiliated with conservative groups and writes on her website that she “honors country tradition while adding relevance and current commentary.”

Patel, who reposted Wilkin’s photo, has faced criticism for traveling on government aircraft on trips that have no known or apparent law enforcement purpose, including using an FBI jet to fly to State College, Pennsylvania, for a pro wrestling event where Wilkins performed the national anthem. Photos posted to social media by Wilkins afterward showed the couple smiling while she held an oversized golden championship belt.

Wilkins also made headlines as a performer at President Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall as part of America 250, as other artists pulled out of the event after finding out it was not a non-partisan celebration.
